name: Northeast Ridge
beta: This is one of the two main routes on Cannon Mountain and is recommended only as an ascent route -- most parties descend via the standard Prusik Pass/Druid Plateau line instead of reversing it. It's best done in mid-to-late summer once snow has melted from around Coney Lake and off the ridge. The route starts at the Stuart Lake Trailhead, climbs steep, bushy, loose burned slopes to the ridge crest, then follows and traverses below the crest -- including a notorious 0.3-mile loose traverse below a band of towers that can't be climbed directly -- before a talus gully and short final scramble to the summit block.
overview: A much harder, more remote alternative to the standard route: a steep, brushy climb up Cannon's north-facing burn slopes to gain the NE ridge crest, followed by sustained class 3 block-scrambling and a loose traverse below a band of unclimbable ridge towers, then a final gully and a short friction move to the summit block.

current.approach: From US-2 at the west end of Leavenworth, follow Icicle Road (Forest Road 7600) about 8 miles, then turn left onto the signed, gravel Eightmile Road. Cross Icicle Creek and climb about 1,100 ft to the large parking area at the road's end (passing the Eightmile Creek Trailhead en route). Northwest Forest Pass required.
approach_variant_names: Eightmile trailhead and the burned slopes to the northeast ridge crest
current.descent: From the summit, head to Prusik Pass and follow the standard route's trail through the Upper Enchantment Basin, down Aasgard Pass, and down the Mountaineer Creek/Colchuck Lake Trail back to the Stuart Lake Trailhead. This is a demanding ~15-mile loop with sustained class 3 scrambling and bushwhacking on the ascent, requiring at least 12 hours car-to-car and an early start.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is used; this is an entirely unroped scramble.
current.pro_needs: None on the standard summer line; an ice axe and crampons only if using the early-season snow-couloir variation around the towers.
bivy: Icicle Creek Road campgrounds near Eightmile Road

name: South Slopes
beta: Cannon has no maintained trail. The most-documented approaches reach a common staging area near Druid Plateau (east of the summit) either from Stuart Lake Trailhead via the Mountaineer Creek valley and Cannon Creek basin (cross-country, brushy lower section with cliff bands), or from the Core Enchantment Zone via Prusik Pass after the longer Snow Lakes Trail approach. From Druid Plateau, parties contour/scramble to the base of the summit block and finish on class 2-3 friction slab and boulders. Snow and verglass can linger on shaded sections into July, adding real exposure to otherwise easy terrain.
overview: Cannon Mountain is a remote Stuart Range summit in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, rising about one mile north of Enchantment Peak on the north side of the core Enchantment Lakes basin, near McClellan Peak and Little Annapurna. First climbed in 1921, it remains one of the least-visited of Washington's 100 highest peaks despite sitting in the middle of the heavily permitted Enchantments, largely because it requires leaving the maintained trail. The standard scramble climbs from Prusik Pass across benches and rock/talus slopes to the 8,350-ft Druid Plateau, crosses the plateau, and finishes on the south side of the summit block via a short friction slab with a natural ramp. While not technically difficult (roughly YDS class 2, with a brief class 3 move to top out the summit boulder), the route demands solid route-finding through brush, benches, and cliff bands, and a big day of elevation gain from either trailhead. The summit gives views across the Enchantment basin to Prusik Peak, Dragontail Peak, and Mount Stuart.

current.approach: Start at the Snow Lakes Trailhead (paved, day-use permit required, ~4 miles up Icicle Creek Road from Leavenworth). Follow the Snow Lakes Trail (#1553) as it climbs through burn-scarred forest and switchbacks above Icicle Creek, passing Nada and Snow Lakes (roughly 6-7 miles in) before continuing up into the core Enchantment Lakes basin — Lake Viviane, then Leprechaun Lake, Sprite Lake, and Perfection Lake. By the time you reach Perfection Lake you have covered on the order of 10-11 miles and about 6,000 ft of gain from the trailhead, all on maintained but rocky, sometimes eroded tread with several creek crossings that can run high with snowmelt in early season. At the north side of Perfection Lake, leave the main trail on the climbers'/scramblers' path that switchbacks up to Prusik Pass (~7,463 ft) — this junction is easy to miss and is the last reliable water before the cross-country section. From Prusik Pass the route leaves all trail: contour northwest across talus and heather benches at roughly 7,300-7,400 ft, staying on the left (west) side of the Lorelei Lakelets, then continue north to a broad rib at about 7,900-8,000 ft. From just below 8,000 ft, turn northwest and climb steep talus/scree (snow-covered into mid-summer) up onto the Druid Plateau (~8,350 ft), where Cannon's summit block comes into view across the plateau. Cross the plateau and take the western slopes to the base of the summit block; the final ~15 ft to the true summit is a low-angle but exposed friction slab climbed via a ramp on the block's south side, with almost no positive holds — approach shoes with good rubber, or rock shoes, make a real difference here. Because the round trip from the trailhead is roughly 30+ miles with 7,300+ ft of gain, essentially all parties camp in or near the core Enchantment zone (competitive overnight permits required in season) rather than attempting it car-to-car; treat the whole cross-country section above Prusik Pass as serious route-finding terrain with no cairns or tread, frequently holding snow into July, and exposed to sun/lightning with no bail-out shelter.
approach_variant_names: Snow Lakes trail to Perfection Lake, Prusik Pass and the Druid Plateau
Stuart Lake trailhead and the Cannon Creek basin — the shorter, rougher side
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the exposed friction-slab ramp off the summit block (often the psychological crux of the day, since downclimbing low-angle slab is harder to read than ascending it), cross back over the Druid Plateau, and pick your way back down the talus/scree slopes to the rib at ~7,900-8,000 ft. From there reverse the contouring traverse at 7,300-7,400 ft past the Lorelei Lakelets to Prusik Pass, then drop back down the scrambler's path to Perfection Lake and rejoin the maintained Snow Lakes Trail for the long hike out past Sprite, Leprechaun, and Viviane Lakes, Snow Lakes, and down to the trailhead. This is a pure scramble/downclimb with no fixed rappel anchors on the standard South Slopes line — no rope or rappel gear is needed for typical summer conditions, though some parties carry a short rope/sling for confidence on the summit block slab. The main descent hazards are the same as the approach in reverse: losing the faint route back to Prusik Pass in whiteout or dusk, loose talus on the plateau slopes, and lingering snow/verglass on the slab or upper gullies in early season, which has turned some ascents into technical downclimbs requiring crampons and careful footwork on rock. A minority of strong parties link Cannon into a longer Enchantments traverse (continuing on to McClellan Peak or exiting via Aasgard Pass to Colchuck Lake) rather than reversing to Snow Lakes, but that is a route variation, not the standard descent.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is needed.
current.pro_needs: There is no protectable climbing on the standard route; this is unroped scrambling. The challenge is navigation and stamina rather than gear.

name: Caravan
beta: Same start as Chitlins Con Carne, but goes straight up after the 3rd bolt into a hard slab crux (5.11b/c) — a step-up move with bolts positioned right at your face — then continues past bolts (5.11-) to chains.
overview: A bolted face route that shares its start with Chitlins Con Carne before breaking right at the third bolt for a hard slab crux to the chains.

current.approach: Summertime Crag uses a different trailhead than the other four areas' shared Blue Lake approach. From Winthrop, drive west on SR-20 through Mazama toward Washington Pass (or, coming from Seattle, continue past Washington Pass toward Mazama on SR-20); park at a small pullout on the east side of the highway, just before the larger 'Spires Gully' parking area used to access the Early Winters Spires from the east. From the pullout, descend off the road down through trees, cross Early Winters Creek, follow it briefly downstream, then climb up-slope and contour left to reach the crag — about a 20-25 minute walk with minimal elevation change. The crag stays shaded until mid-afternoon in summer, making it a popular warm-weather alternative when Mazama-area cragging runs hot.
current.descent: Lower or make a single-rope rappel from the top chains back to the base; reverse the approach to return to the car.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted; standard quickdraw sport rack (bolts are positioned right at the crux slab move).
current.pro_needs: No trad gear required — bolts only.

name: Southeast Slopes
beta: From a basin camp roughly 6,800–7,100 ft below the peak, parties cross moderate snow/scree slopes toward the saddle between the north and middle summits, then follow the summit ridge (Class 2-3, with a couple of steep snow patches early season) to the non-technical middle summit (~8,590 ft). Reaching the true, slightly higher south summit requires a short, exposed technical step (unrated low 5th class / easy mixed moves) that most guided descriptions treat as the crux; many scramblers stop at the middle summit rather than commit to it. When the north side holds snow, parties commonly drop onto the east/southeast slopes below the summit ridge (this route) rather than fight the icier north ridge.
overview: Cardinal Peak (8,596 ft) is the highest summit in the Chelan Mountains, a remote subrange at the head of the Entiat River drainage, less than 5 miles from Lake Chelan. The peak has three summit points along its ridge; the standard route reaches the middle summit, traditionally treated as the highpoint, via a gully and ridge on the mountain's west side — though a June 2023 theodolite survey found the south summit is roughly 7 inches taller and is technically the true highpoint, reached from the middle summit by a short, exposed low-5th-class step that this route includes as an optional finish. The north summit is a separate, harder Class 4 objective and is rarely climbed. Roughly 95% of climbers use the same North Fork Entiat approach, camping in the basin below Cardinal, Emerald, and Saska Peaks before a Class 3 scramble with real exposure near the top.

current.approach: From the end of FR-5606 (the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, ~3,940 ft), pick up the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437. This lower section sits outside wilderness, so mountain bikes are legal and commonly used to knock out easy miles. The first ~6 miles follow the North Fork Entiat River on a gentle, mostly forested grade, with the river itself as a reliable water source the whole way — top off here, since the route runs dry above. Some post-wildfire sections have significant blowdown; a few parties describe losing the tread briefly among downed timber and having to scramble back onto it. At about mile 6.1 a signed spur splits off to Fern Lake (Trail #1436) — stay on #1437. Around mile 7, at roughly 5,800 ft, the main trail bends sharply east and climbs switchbacks for about a half mile to a junction with the Pyramid Mountain Trail #1433 at about 6,600 ft, roughly a mile southwest of Cardinal's summit and a useful timing landmark. The final approach mile above this junction is noted as steep and loose underfoot. From the open meadow/basin past the junction, leave the trail and hike east through sparse forest, then talus, toward Cardinal's west/southwest flank. For the Southeast Slopes line specifically, contour or drop onto the peak's western slopes and work south below the summit ridge across steep talus and scree to reach the gully leading to the notch between the north and middle (traditionally climbed) summits — the same scree-gully notch most parties use regardless of which flank they approach from. Loose rock is constant in the upper basin and gully, so a helmet is worthwhile and parties should avoid stacking up directly below one another. Round trip to the summit runs roughly 20-21 miles with about 4,700 ft of gain, so most parties do it as a long single day or a one-night backpack with camp in the meadows/basin below the peak. The trail crosses Grouse Creek on a log partway up, within one of the fire-damaged sections that has blowdown.
approach_variant_names: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the Pyramid Mountain junction, then the west-side basin
current.descent: This is a walk-down/downclimb — no rope work or anchors are needed on the Southeast Slopes line. Reverse the ascent: downclimb the loose scree gully from the notch back into the upper basin, then pick your way back down through talus and sparse forest to rejoin the North Fork Entiat Trail near the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction (~6,600 ft). From there it's a straightforward trail descent down the switchbacks to about 5,800 ft and out along the gentle lower six-plus miles back to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead. The scree gully is the main descent hazard — it's loose top to bottom, so descend deliberately, keep the group tight, and stay alert for rockfall triggered by climbers above. One trip report on this peak noted the descent taking roughly half the time of the ascent once back on established trail. No rappels are required on this route.
current.detailed_rack: Primarily an unroped scramble. A light rack (a few small cams/nuts and slings) and a 30m rope are worth carrying for the short technical step guarding the true summit, though most parties simply downclimb it unroped.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection reported. Any gear carried is only for the optional short technical step below the true summit, on sound granodiorite/quartz diorite.
bivy: West-side basin camp below Cardinal Peak
The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
current.rope_note: Class 3 scramble via SE/E slopes to a notch below the summit block. No rope needed for the middle-summit walkup; the true south summit register requires 4th/5th class moves where some parties choose a short handline.

name: Carne Mountain Trail
beta: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead, follow the wide Phelps Creek Trail for about a quarter mile, then bear right and steeply uphill onto the narrower, unmaintained-feel Carne Mountain Trail (#1508). It climbs via moderate-to-steep switchbacks through forest and across an open talus slope for roughly 2.5-2.9 miles to a small alpine basin (~6,100 ft) with campsites and a stream. From there the trail continues to a low pass/junction with the Old Gib Trail around mile 3, then climbs to a saddle (~6,800 ft) with views of Mount Maude, Clark Mountain, and Glacier Peak, before a final quarter mile along the ridge to the 7,085 ft summit.
overview: Carne Mountain (~7,080–7,085 ft) is the Entiat Mountains' most popular day-hike summit, reached by a steep, well-built trail that climbs out of the Phelps Creek valley (not from its head — the route branches off just 0.4 mile from the trailhead). It is famous for one of Washington's finest golden-larch displays in late September/early October and for sweeping views of Glacier Peak, Mount Maude, Fortress Mountain, and Bandit Peak. A fire lookout once stood on the south (lower) summit; only the site remains, and the true high point is the north summit reached via a use path along the ridge.

current.approach: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (~3,500 ft, end of FR 6211), start on the wide, gently graded Phelps Creek Trail #1511 heading north/upstream along Phelps Creek through open forest. In roughly 0.25–0.4 mile, watch for a signed junction and bear right (steeply uphill) onto the narrower Carne Mountain Trail — this is the last easy water for a while, so top off here or at the small creeklet just past the junction, since the climb above is essentially dry except for early-season snowmelt. From the junction the trail wastes no time, switchbacking up through open forest, vine maple, and beargrass slopes and gaining about 2,600 ft in the next 2.9 miles — a sustained, steep grade with little flat respite. Around 3.1–3.2 miles from the trailhead you top out at a broad saddle near 6,800 ft with a sweeping view of Mount Maude, Seven Fingered Jack, Clark Mountain, and Glacier Peak; this saddle is also the junction with the climbers'/unmaintained Rock Creek Trail heading east. From the saddle, bear left and switchback up open talus and scree for a final 0.4–0.5 mile to the summit at 7,091 ft, passing near a minor false high point along the way. The standard route is Class 1–2 the entire way (a steep trail/talus walk, no technical scrambling), but snow can linger on the upper switchbacks and around the saddle into early-mid July, and the exposed saddle/ridge can be windy — an ice axe is worth carrying for early-season snow patches near the top. There is no ford of Phelps Creek on this route (the trail junction is well before any major crossing); the only route-finding subtlety is picking the correct fork at the Phelps Creek/Carne Mountain junction low down and staying on-trail through the talus near the summit block.
approach_variant_names: Phelps Creek Trail to the Carne Mountain Trail #1508 fork
current.descent: This is a walk-off — reverse the ascent trail all the way back to the Phelps Creek Trailhead. No rappelling or technical downclimbing is involved on the standard route; the only care needed is on the steep upper switchbacks and talus near the saddle if snow or loose scree is present, and general Class 2 talus-walking care on the final push off the summit. Parties wanting a longer, more strenuous alternative descent (or ascent) can instead traverse east from the 6,800-ft saddle past Point 7103 toward Ice Lakes and drop into Leroy Basin, following Leroy Creek's trail back down to the Phelps Creek Trail and out — but that loop adds significant mileage and about 1,200 ft more cumulative gain (roughly 16 mi / 4,800 ft total versus the ~7.3 mi / 3,600 ft standard out-and-back), so it is a distinct high-route variant rather than the default descent.
bivy: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
current.rope_note: Maintained hiking trail to a ridge walk, Class 1-2. No technical gear required at any point.

name: East Ridge and NW Chimney
beta: Class 4-low 5th alpine rock route up Cascade Peak own short, broken summit tower via the NW Chimney -- reached via the same CJ Couloir most parties use to approach neighboring Johannesburg Mountain East Ridge. Roughly 3 pitches (a loose, wide crux crack, the 5.8 chimney, then a short, very loose finish) on consistently loose, broken rock with essentially no fixed protection or rappel anchors. Expect real routefinding, not a clean traveled line.
overview: A scenic alpine route combining the East Ridge and Northwest Chimney on Cascade Peak, typically done as a single enchainment via the CJ Couloir approach. The route offers varied climbing and excellent views of the North Cascades Highway corridor.

current.approach: Start from the Cascade Pass Road trailhead (elevation 3,600 ft). Hike to the base of the CJ Couloir (approximately 0.7 mi). Enter the couloir and ascend to the East Ridge proper. The route then transitions to the NW Chimney section for the final approach to the summit.
approach_variant_names: Up the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir to the C-J col
Cascade Pass, Mixup Arm and the Cache Glacier
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb/simul-climb back to the top of the technical pitches, then rappel the NW Chimney to the moat using gear anchors you build as you go (bring doubles for full-length raps — there is no fixed hardware on this route). Traverse back to the C-J col and reverse the CJ Couloir (roughly 3,400 ft of downclimbing/rappelling on snow and ice) to the base near the Cascade River, then retrace the short bushwhack and road walk to the trailhead. Avoid the 'Doug's Direct' descent some older references mention off the col — at least one detailed trip report calls it a miserable, circuitous heather-and-rock traverse that took longer than simply reversing the couloir.
current.detailed_rack: For the NW Chimney: a single rack of nuts plus something wide — a Big Bro or a large cam — for the loose 5-6" crux crack; a 2013 ascent party carried only 7-8 nuts and found solid placements scarce on the first pitch. Bring 60m doubles so you can build and rappel full-length off your own anchors back to the moat; there are no fixed rap stations on this route.
current.pro_needs: Protection on the NW Chimney is sparse and the rock is loose and broken; the crux pitch offers only a couple of solid nut placements in a wide, rotten crack, so a large cam or Big Bro helps. There are no established rappel anchors anywhere on the route — plan to build your own on the way down and expect to leave some gear behind.

name: Northwest Chimney
beta: Graded 5.8, the Northwest Chimney climbs three pitches of broken, loose rock - including an aesthetic but sparsely-protected chimney pitch - from the moat below the peak's northwest side to the summit. Loose rock can make the crux first pitch feel considerably harder than that grade (closer to 5.10), and no rappel anchors, pitons or summit register have been reported, which suggests the route sees very few ascents.
overview: A serious three-pitch rock line up Cascade Peak's northwest side, approached from the C-J col; loose rock and minimal fixed protection make it a rarely-repeated, committing alternative to the East Ridge scramble.

current.approach: Same approach as the East Ridge to the C-J col (Cascade River Road to Cascade Pass Trailhead, Cascade Pass Trail to Cascade Pass, then cross-country via Mixup Arm/Cache Glacier to the C-J col). From a bivy at the col, cross the moat below Cascade Peak's northwest side to reach the base of the route.
approach_variant_names: Bivy at the C-J col, then across the moat onto the peak's northwest side
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb/simul-climb back to the top of the technical pitches and rappel the route on gear-built nut/cam anchors. Allow roughly 4.5 hours from the summit back to the C-J col.
current.detailed_rack: Roughly 7-8 nuts, extra slings, and doubled key cam sizes for building rappel anchors, plus a large offset/"Big Bro"-style piece for the chimney pitch (per a 2013 trip report).
current.pro_needs: Sparse and unreliable - loose rock limits gear placements; expect to build cam/nut anchors from scratch for each rappel rather than relying on fixed gear.

name: SE Route
beta: From the Eightmile Trail, cut cross-country up through an old burn zone, then continue up and left toward the gully between the S and SE ridges. The S/SE gully is wide and offers a 'choose your own adventure' character: the center/right line is mostly class 2, while the climbers-left side holds solid class 3-4 rock. The gully tops out at roughly 8,150 ft, about 360 vertical feet below the 8,501 ft top. This line cuts the standard 8-9 mile one-way West Ridge approach roughly in half.
overview: A faster alternative to the standard West Ridge: leaves the Eightmile Trail early to go cross-country up Cashmere's southeast slopes, roughly halving the round-trip mileage before finishing up a broad gully between the south and southeast ridges.

current.approach: Leave the Eightmile Trail onto an old logging road, then boot up an ashen, deadfall-choked burn-zone hillside for about 1,000 ft of gain. Above the burn, continue cross-country up and left toward the SE gullies, crossing a snowfield before reaching the base of the S/SE gully; expect some brief bushwhacking, loose steep dirt, and side-hilling/boulder-hopping en route.
approach_variant_names: Eightmile Trail, old logging road and the burn
current.descent: Reverse the ascent. Downclimb the SE gully, mostly class 2-3, staying in the main gully rather than drifting left onto harder ground, which is easy to do in fog. At the foot of the gullies a snowfield leads down; early in the season it is firm in the morning and may call for crampons, and by afternoon it softens enough to boot-ski or plunge-step. Below it, the burned hillside of ash and deadfall is the slowest part going up but quick coming down by plunge-stepping, and it leads back to the old logging road and the Eightmile Trail. No rappels are needed.
current.detailed_rack: No rope or rack is used; this is an unroped class 2-3 (locally class 3-4) scramble.
current.pro_needs: None - climbed unroped as a scramble.

name: West Ridge
beta: The standard and easiest route on Cashmere Mountain. From Windy Pass the west ridge becomes the obvious line: descend to a saddle where the scrambling begins, then work through a series of tooth-like gendarmes separated by roughly five main gaps, weaving from the north side of the ridge to the south and back, rarely following the crest exactly. Cairns mark parts of the route but route-finding is required. Rock is generally solid granite but loose in spots near the summit; snow or rime can turn the Class 3 terrain into harder Class 4 climbing in early season or after storms, and parties have roped up with slings/chocks for running belays in those conditions.
overview: Cashmere Mountain (8,501 ft), first climbed in 1900 by USGS surveyor Robert A. Farmer, is a high-prominence summit of the Wenatchee Mountains rising north of the Enchantments core above the Icicle Creek drainage. The standard West Ridge route is a long approach (roughly 17 miles round trip with about 5,300-5,500 ft of gain from the Eightmile Lake trailhead) leading to real, exposed scrambling: the upper ridge narrows into a series of tooth-like gendarmes separated by five main notches, and the final several hundred feet to the summit climb a northwest-facing gully system with sustained class 3 and a few exposed class 4 moves -- this is not a simple talus walk. Most parties camp at Lake Caroline or Little Lake Caroline (inside the Eightmile/Caroline zone of the Enchantment Permit Area, which requires an overnight permit) to split the long day. The summit gives sweeping views over the core Enchantment peaks (Prusik, Dragontail, Colchuck) and the Stuart Range to the south, and Cashmere's prominence makes it a popular peak-bagging objective (58th on the Washington Bulger list).

current.approach: From the Eightmile Lake Trailhead (~3,300 ft, reached via Icicle Creek Road and Road 7601/Eightmile Road as in the drive note), start on the Eightmile Lake Trail (Trail #1552). The trail climbs through partly burned forest and brushy slopes for about 2.8 miles to a junction just past Little Eightmile Lake (~4,400 ft) — this is the last easy water before the high country. At the junction, branch right (north) onto the Eightmile–Trout Creek Trail (Trail #1554), signed toward Lake Caroline. Follow this roughly 2.25–2.75 miles to Lake Caroline, then continue about 0.5 mile to Little Lake Caroline; both lakes sit inside the Enchantments Permit Area, so a permit is required for any overnight camping here. From Little Lake Caroline, continue about 0.8 mile toward Windy Pass (~7,220 ft). Around 6,850 ft, leave the maintained trail and head cross-country to the east, climbing gently; good bivy/camp options appear about 0.5 mile and 250 vertical feet later, around 7,100 ft — this is the last reliable water and the usual high camp for a two-day trip (strong parties push it in a single long car-to-car day, reported at up to ~17 miles round trip). From camp, climb NNE to the broad col on the west side of Cashmere Mountain (~8,000 ft), then follow the west ridge itself up to about 8,200 ft. From there, make a rising traverse/contour several hundred yards around to the northwest side of the summit pyramid to a northwest-facing gully; this gully leads to the summit. The upper ridge is a series of tooth-like gendarmes separated by roughly five main notches, and the route weaves back and forth between the north and south sides of the crest rather than following it directly — expect real route-finding, a short snowfield crossing below Windy Pass in early season (an axe/microspikes are worth carrying through mid-summer), and loose, blocky rock with some exposure on the class 3–4 scrambling that begins near the col and continues to the summit.
approach_variant_names: Eightmile Lake to Lake Caroline and Windy Pass
current.descent: Descend by reversing the West Ridge exactly as ascended: downclimb the northwest-facing summit gully back to the ~8,200 ft contour, follow the ridge back down through the same notches/gendarmes to the 8,000 ft west col, then drop SSW back to the ~7,100 ft camp/cross-country section and rejoin the Trail #1554/Windy Pass trail. From there retrace the Eightmile–Trout Creek Trail past Lake Caroline and Little Eightmile Lake back onto Trail #1552 to the Eightmile Lake Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappels are used on the standard West Ridge route; every description of this line treats it as a reversal of the ascent. The class 3–4 sections are the main descent hazard: the ridge's loose, blocky rock and exposed ledges are more consequential to downclimb than to ascend, and it's easy to drift onto the wrong (steeper) side of the crest while trying to retrace the weaving north/south line through the notches — many parties downclimb the steepest short sections (roughly the last 50 ft below each notch) facing in, one at a time. Afternoon thunderstorm exposure on the long, open ridge and glissade-able but firm early-season snow near Windy Pass are the other things to plan around; there is no technical descent gear (rope, rack, or anchors) needed for the standard route.
current.detailed_rack: No fixed rack is required for the standard dry-season Class 3 scramble; parties occasionally carry a small selection of slings and a few small-to-medium chocks/nuts for optional running-belay protection on exposed sections or when snow/rime is present.
current.pro_needs: There is no protectable climbing on the standard scramble; movement is unroped. Navigation and endurance are the real demands.
current.rope_note: Unroped scramble; rope optional for snow/glacier sections

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Castle Peak's standard ascent is a granite scramble featuring mostly Class 2 terrain with sections of easy Class 3. Rock quality is excellent and reminiscent of the Stuart Range. Route-finding is required in micro-terrain and sections are steep with krummholz. The peak can be approached from three main directions, all requiring significant approach commitment.
overview: Castle Peak (8,343 ft; a 2020s survey pegged it at 8343.4 ft +/- 0.2 ft) is the second-highest summit in the Hozameen Range after Jack Mountain and the 6th-highest peak in the Pasayten Wilderness, about 1 mile south of the Canada-US border on the Cascade crest (Okanogan/Whatcom county line). With roughly 3,263 ft of prominence it ranks 42nd in Washington and is one of the state's most remote high-prominence summits (distinct from the Tatoosh Range's Castle Peak). It is granite; the peak's steep north face holds several technical routes up to IV 5.10+ A1 (e.g. 'The Drawbridge'; the north face proper was first climbed by Beckey-Nolting-Tindall in 1979), while the standard route is an unroped class 2-3 scramble up the southwest side, reached by long, remote approaches.

current.approach: This route starts with a boat crossing of Ross Lake (Ross Lake Resort water taxi, or a private/inflatable boat carried in via the 0.6-mile portage trail from the SR-20 pullout), landing at the Lightning Creek Trailhead near the head of the lake at roughly 1,500 ft. From the shoreline, follow the Lightning Creek Trail north; parties with their own boat commonly start pre-dawn (around 4am) to leave enough daylight for the long day above, while the water taxi runs only from 8am to 5pm. After about 2 hours of hiking, watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek Trail. The first stretch above the junction is the trickiest routefinding on the whole approach: steep rock-and-alder slopes that require a rising, diagonal ascent line before you regain proper forest and trail tread — recent parties note intermittent orange flagging tape marking this stretch, which is worth watching for. Once back in the trees, tread on the Freezeout Creek Trail improves to 'decent shape' as you climb to the Freezeout Cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited immediately after a creek crossing; the cabin (maintained bunks, wood stove, logbook) is a good psychological waypoint and emergency shelter. About a quarter mile past the cabin, cross Freezeout Creek again and pass through an old burn. Trail tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft, but the bushwhacking through here is described as minimal. From there, stay on the west side of Freezeout Creek, hiking roughly 50-100 ft above the waterline, which gives the most open going through 5,000 ft. At 5,000 ft, cross to the south/east side of the drainage, where the terrain opens into meadow and talus. Above this, climb steep red heather, talus, and scree to a notch on the peak's southwest ridge at about 7,600 ft. From the notch, the final roughly 700-750 vertical feet to the 8,300+ ft summit is class 2 with short class 3 sections. Total one-way distance from the lakeshore to the summit is on the order of 16-17 miles with close to 7,000 ft of gain from the boat landing alone (the 8,500 ft gain figure reflects the day's cumulative up-and-down, not just net elevation). Freezeout Creek is the reliable water source for essentially the entire approach up to about 5,000-5,500 ft; carry water above that, since there is no dependable source on the upper heather/talus/scree slopes or the summit ridge. Because of the remoteness and boat-access logistics, this is realistically a long single push (18+ hours car-to-car including the taxi) or a one-night backpack, not a casual day hike.
approach_variant_names: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek trail and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail
The crest trail north from Harts Pass to Castle Pass
current.descent: There is no rappelling on this route — it is a walk-off/downclimb descent that simply reverses the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb the class 2-3 ground back to the notch on the southwest ridge at ~7,600 ft, then descend the same steep heather/talus/scree slope back into the Freezeout Creek drainage. This is the point where parties get into trouble: the upper basin has several gullies and chutes that look similar from above, and dropping into the wrong one risks cliffing out on bluffs well above the creek — stick to the exact ascent gully rather than improvising a shortcut. Cross back to the west side of Freezeout Creek at about 5,000 ft, follow the creek down through the old burn, rejoin the Freezeout Creek Trail tread around 4,200 ft, pass back through the cabin at 3,600 ft, and continue down to the abandoned lower Freezeout Creek Trail / Lightning Creek Trail junction, watching again for the flagged diagonal line through the steep rock-and-alder section. Finish on the Lightning Creek Trail back to the Ross Lake shoreline for the return boat/water-taxi pickup. Because of the length of the day, parties commonly finish this descent in the dark (one party that brought its own boat reached the lakeshore around 11:30pm after a roughly 4am start; the water taxi runs only from 8am to 5pm), so carry headlamps and treat the unmaintained trail sections and creek crossings with extra caution when tired and in low light. Other hazards on the way down include loose, ball-bearing-like scree on the upper slopes (slip/fall risk), the creek crossings themselves if water is high, and afternoon thunderstorm/lightning exposure on the open summit ridge and upper basin — get off the ridge before storms build.
current.detailed_rack: Small rack (cams/nuts) optional for Class 3+ crux sections. Most ascents done without protection on the standard route. Natural ledges and rock features can serve as emergency belay points if needed, but protection is rarely deployed on ascent.
current.pro_needs: Unroped class 2-3 scramble; no technical gear normally required. The north face holds separate technical routes (up to IV 5.10+ A1) that are outside the scope of this standard scramble route.
current.rope_note: Class 2 with easy Class 3 and a few Class 3+ steps on solid granite. No rope on the standard scramble; carry an ice axe if snow patches persist near the 7600' notch.

name: South Route
beta: Distinct from the East Ridge Couloir/Southeast Ridge line, this route stays on the peak's south side. From a camp near 5,500 ft in Castle Creek Basin, ascend the wide gully on the south side to about 6,800 ft, then enter the northeast gully aiming for a notch around 7,400 ft. The final section crosses granite slabs, boulders and snow patches with a short scramble to the true summit.
overview: An alternate, US-side non-technical line up Castle Peak from Castle Creek Basin, climbing a wide south-facing gully to a northeast gully and a roughly 7,400-ft notch high on the mountain, then a short scramble to the summit.

current.approach: The line most often written up starts on the Monument 78 Trail in Manning Park, BC and crosses the US/Canada border in the boundary clearing south of Castle Creek; entering the US on foot away from a port of entry is not lawful, so the lawful way in is the long walk north on the PCT from Harts Pass to Castle Pass at the head of Castle Creek. As written up, the Canadian line continues: Cross the Castle Creek bridge, push south through brush and downed timber, navigate the boundary clearing and wetland openings, then follow Castle Creek uphill from about 4,500 ft through alder terrain to a camp around 5,500 ft in Castle Creek Basin.
approach_variant_names: The crest trail north from Harts Pass to Castle Pass, then the head of Castle Creek
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line back through the notch, northeast gully and south gully to Castle Creek Basin camp.

name: La Villa
beta: A 5.7 trad route in The Castle's climbing area alongside the easy-5th-class Southeast Face; no detailed pitch-by-pitch description, approach specifics, or first-ascent history is on record. Likely approached the same way as the Southeast Face — via the Pinnacle Peak Trail from Reflection Lakes and a traverse across Pinnacle's south-face scree to the Castle-Pinnacle area.
overview: A three-star, low-fifth-class trad line in the small rock-climbing area on The Castle, distinct from (and reportedly higher quality than) the standard scramble/chimney route to the summit.

current.approach: Same as the Southeast Face: from Reflection Lakes (4,859 ft), take the Pinnacle Peak Trail 1.3 miles to the Pinnacle–Plummer saddle, then contour across Pinnacle's south-face scree/talus to the base of Castle's southeast side and scramble up broken ground to reach the base of the summit block. During the Plummer Peak Fire the park closed the Butter Creek Research Natural Area, south of the Pinnacle Peak Trail to the park boundary; its edge runs along the crest at The Castle, so Castle's south side and the east end of this traverse are off limits while that closure stands. Check the park's fire and closure notices before you go.
approach_variant_names: Reflection Lakes and the Pinnacle traverse to the taller summit spire
current.descent: From the belay ledge atop La Villa, traverse rightward (climber's right) past the true summit to the heavily-trafficked low-5th topout area shared with the Southeast Face route, where fixed slings are typically already in place. Make a single ~40 ft (12 m) rappel back to the base of the technical section, downclimb the 3rd-class terrain below, and reverse the scree traverse and Pinnacle Peak Trail back to Reflection Lakes.
current.detailed_rack: A rack to 3 inches with medium cams, nuts and slings. One solid medium cam protects the three slabby 5.8 crux moves and the rest of the pitch takes little gear.
current.pro_needs: One solid medium cam protects the three slabby 5.8 crux moves; the rest of the pitch takes little gear.
current.rope_note: 40m rope standard for this harder route

name: Southeast Face (Standard Route)
beta: From the Pinnacle Saddle Trailhead at Reflection Lakes, hike the Pinnacle Peak Trail to the ~5,920-ft saddle between Pinnacle Peak and Plummer Peak, then leave the trail and contour east across Pinnacle's south-face scree/talus (roughly 6,000-6,200 ft) to the Castle-Pinnacle col. From the col, scramble onto Castle's south rib, make a short class-3 traverse onto the east flank, and follow the obvious crack-chimney system (easy 5th class; some parties call this the East Face Chimney Route) up and right to a notch beside a natural rock horn. A brief, exposed class 3-4 scramble along the summit crest leads to the true (northernmost) summit block. Many parties fix a handline or belay the chimney pitch and always rappel or downclimb it on the return.
overview: Castle Peak's easiest and by far most-traveled line: a class 2-3 approach and traverse around Pinnacle Peak's south flank to the Castle-Pinnacle col, followed by a short, well-protected easy-5th-class crack-and-chimney pitch up the southeast/east flank to the exposed summit crest.

current.approach: Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road (or, when the road is snowed in, at the year-round Narada Falls lot). Take the signed Pinnacle Peak Trail from the south side of the road; it climbs steadily through forest and subalpine meadow for about 1.3 miles and 1,050 ft of gain to the 5,920-ft saddle between Pinnacle Peak and Plummer Peak. From the saddle, instead of continuing up Pinnacle, traverse climber's-left (east) across Pinnacle's south-facing scree/boulder field, staying around 6,000-6,200 ft, to the col between Pinnacle and Castle — roughly another half mile of cross-country travel to the base of Castle's south/southeast side. During the Plummer Peak Fire the park closed the Butter Creek Research Natural Area, south of the Pinnacle Peak Trail to the park boundary; its edge runs along the crest at The Castle, so Castle's south side and the east end of this traverse are off limits while that closure stands. Check the park's fire and closure notices before you go.
approach_variant_names: Reflection Lakes, Pinnacle Saddle and the scree traverse east to the Castle-Pinnacle col
current.descent: From the true summit, downclimb the short, exposed crest back to the notch above the crack-chimney pitch. Most parties rappel from a sturdy natural rock horn/block near the notch back down to the base of the technical section (carry your own webbing/rap rings rather than relying on tat left by other groups). From there, downclimb the class-3 section back onto the south rib, retrace the contouring traverse across Pinnacle's scree slope to the Pinnacle-Castle col and back to the main saddle, then descend the Pinnacle Peak Trail to Reflection Lakes. In winter and spring the same line is often skied or glissaded from the col.
current.detailed_rack: Full set up to #2 Camalot, or doubles in finger-to-mid-sized cams; Full set of stoppers
current.pro_needs: Protection is sparse on the chimney/crack pitch — a handful of finger-to-hand-sized cams and stoppers covers it, and the rest of the route takes little gear.
bivy: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle

name: Northeast Ridge (2003 Variation)
beta: Put up by Mike Preiss and Mark Bunker in 2003. It starts where the original Northeast Ridge route ends its first pitch. From there, traverse left and up through scary, unstable Class 4+ rock on a short pitch, aiming for a left-hand vertical crack in a left-facing corner identified by yellow-speckled rock with roofs above. The third pitch follows that crack and exits over its left side — the route's best pitch, rated 5.7/5.8 and well protected. Above, the rock eases and parties navigate upward through variations, with a short difficult left-leaning crack at 5.9+ before moderate terrain leads to the summit area. It carries a PG13 protection rating and would deserve a higher star rating were it not for the precarious second pitch.
overview: A six-pitch, 1,000-foot Grade III 5.9 variation that branches off where the original Northeast Ridge finishes its first pitch, taking a left-facing corner with a vertical crack through yellow-speckled rock and roofs. The best pitch on the route is a well-protected 5.7/5.8 crack; the second pitch's scary, unstable Class 4+ rock is what holds the route back.

current.approach: Drive to the Cathedral Rock trailhead (Trail #1345, ~3,350 ft) via I-90 Exit 80, SR-903 north through Roslyn and Ronald about 14.8 miles, then 12.3 miles of gravel Cle Elum Valley Road / FR 4330 and the NF-153 spur. Sign the free wilderness permit at the register. Hike trail #1345 past Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake, ~4,850 ft) at 2.5 miles to the Cathedral Pass / PCT junction at 5,550 ft, 4 miles in. From there the northeast side is reached the same way as the Northeast Buttress: cut across the meadow to the stand of trees (a good gear cache), then traverse under the east face across talus toward the northeast side of the peak. Note that this route begins from the top of the original Northeast Ridge route's first pitch.
approach_variant_names: Cathedral Pass, the gear-cache trees, and the traverse to the original route's first pitch
current.descent: From the summit area, descend the south side rather than reversing the ridge. Scramble the Class 2-3 crest southwest to the top of the Southwest Face crux, make one or two rappels using the rock horn with fixed slings and rings (inspect and back it up), downclimb the main gully — the loosest ground of the day — and contour southeast across talus and heather to Cathedral Pass. Pick up any cached gear on the way back around to the trail. The south side sees more traffic and so carries less loose rock than the northeast, which is why it is the usual descent for the peak. Allow 2-3 hours summit to pass, plus 1.5-2 hours down trail #1345.
current.detailed_rack: Medium rock protection up to 4+ inches and runners. In practice: a single set of nuts, cams from small through 4 inches (with the larger sizes for the left-facing corner and the left-leaning crack), and a generous set of alpine draws and double-length runners for slinging blocks and horns and for keeping drag manageable on a wandering line. Two ropes, or one 60m plus a tag, so that bailing from the middle of the route is possible. Spare slings and rap rings.
current.pro_needs: The route is rated PG13. The crux third pitch — the vertical crack in the left-facing corner — is described as well protected and is the best pitch on the climb; the problem is the short second pitch of scary, unstable Class 4+ rock leading to it, where the protection and the rock quality are both poor. The short 5.9+ left-leaning crack higher up is the other place where gear matters. Elsewhere the rock eases and the climbing is moderate. Sling solid features in preference to placing cams in the fractured andesite.

name: Northwest Couloir
beta: The Northwest Couloir climbs to a chockstone in the upper gully; parties commonly rappel or downclimb past the chockstone. Some parties descend it back toward Peggy's Pond, but the standard descent from the summit is the Southwest Face. The couloir holds notably loose, fractured rock.
overview: A class 3 gully on Cathedral Rock's northwest side, used as an alternate ascent line and, by some parties, as a descent back toward Peggy's Pond.

current.approach: Approached the same way as the Southwest Face route, via Salmon la Sac, Forest Road 4330, and the Cathedral Rock trail to Cathedral Pass, then around toward the northwest side of the summit block. In September a cairned line crosses heather benches up the west shoulder to the couloir base; the steep loose talus alternative is slower. Going counter-clockwise round Peggy Pond reaches the rock field by a path; traversing high and clockwise through steep heather is much worse.
current.descent: One way down is to reverse the route, downclimbing the chimney and couloir and then descending via separate open books and scree slopes back to Peggy's Pond; there is a rappel ring anchor (and an old piton) near the top. If you are reversing the couloir, treat the chockstone chimney as the crux of the descent and rappel it rather than fighting it downwards with a pack. The alternative — and the better option if you are heading for the trailhead rather than a camp at the pond — is to descend the ordinary Southwest Face: scramble the ridge crest southwest, make one or two rappels off the rock horn with fixed slings and rings, downclimb the main gully, and walk back to Cathedral Pass. Either way, inspect any fixed anchor you find; the tat and hardware on this peak is old.
current.detailed_rack: Minimal. A short rope, a few nuts and cams to 3 inches for the chimney and any belays you decide to build, and half a dozen long runners for slinging chockstones and horns. A rappel device and a couple of spare slings and rap rings to replace or back up the fixed anchor near the top.
current.pro_needs: The route is Class 3, so most parties move unroped over most of it, but the chockstone chimney and the upper friction slab are the two places where a rope is worth having, and the slab in particular offers very little to place — the large flake used as a handrail is the main feature. Slinging chockstones in the couloir gives the most reliable anchors on this rock.
bivy: Peggy's Pond — standard base camp and water source

name: Chair-Bryant Traverse
beta: Pitch-by-pitch beta for this line is not available. It begins on Chair's north ridge and follows the crest toward Bryant on 4th-class to low-5th-class rock, with one short, steep mandatory rappel (~50 ft) getting off Bryant — the same rappel found on the closely related 'Tooth - Chair Traverse,' which covers the Bryant-to-Chair portion of this ridge system.
overview: An alpine ridge linkup that starts on Chair Peak's north ridge and follows the crest toward Bryant Peak, with parties often extending the traverse further to The Tooth or even Denny Mountain for a longer high-route day.

current.approach: Begins on Chair Peak's north ridge, reached via the East Face/Northeast Buttress approach (Alpental parking, Snow Lake Trail, Source Lake fork, then a gully to roughly 4,800 ft and the basin below), then continues along the crest over/past Bryant Peak.
current.descent: Typically descend from wherever the traverse is exited (Bryant, the Tooth, or Denny) via that peak's own standard descent, since reversing the ridge crest is slow and exposed.

name: East Face
beta: Rated 5.2 (PG13) over 3 pitches, 600 ft (182 m); about 400 ft of the route's pleasant climbing is 4th to easy 5th class, with the notable overhanging band rated 5.5. Protection is sparse in places, with runouts over 50 ft reported on the traverse pitch.
overview: A moderate 3rd-to-low-5th-class rock line directly up the east face to the summit, one of the more accessible summer scrambling/climbing routes on the peak, with a well-known overhanging band crux.

current.approach: From the Alpental parking lot, take the Snow Lake Trail; at about 1.5 miles turn off toward Source Lake. Ascend a 3rd-class rocky gully starting around 4,200 ft, reach a small cliff around 4,800 ft, traverse through a notch, then cross a snowy basin to the base of the route around 5,500 ft. In August the turn toward the east-face basin comes just after the first switchback above Source Lake, marked by a cairn; a faint path climbs the dry waterfall gully, then trees lead to the talus field below the face.
approach_variant_names: Source Lake and the WNW gully into the east-face basin
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb and traverse back toward the notch area, locate the marked south-facing rappel gully (the southern chimney), and make two single-rope rappels down the chimney and a third down the steep, narrow snow finger below it to return to the approach basin. Going down the south gully, skip the first slung gully and the single sling on a boulder; head for the trees below, where four 60 m rappels reach the base, and watch for rockfall at the last station tucked behind an overhang.
current.detailed_rack: Light alpine rock rack: small nuts, cams from about 0.2 to 2 in (a #3 optional), several single- and double-length slings, a cordelette for anchors at ledges, plus extra webbing and rap rings for the descent anchors.
current.pro_needs: Protection is good on pitch 1 (chimney/crack) but sparse and runout on pitch 2's traverse, where placements can be more than 50 ft apart; the upper 3rd/4th-class terrain takes little gear. Build solid anchors at stances with a cordelette and slings.

name: North Face
beta: Reached via a short traverse from the Source Lake-Snow Lake divide, the North Face offers about four pitches of steep snow and ice climbing on generally moderate-angle terrain (50-65°) with one short crux step that can approach 80° (sometimes rock, 5.4-5.6, if thin on ice). Abundant natural/fixed protection and a short approach make it a popular introduction to Cascade ice climbing, though it backs up with parties on clear winter weekends. Note: a distinct, harder rock variation called 'North Face Direct' (5.9, 5 pitches) starts about 200m from the standard line and should not be confused with this route.
overview: Chair Peak's North Face is one of Washington's most popular winter alpine ice-and-mixed classics, easily reached from Snoqualmie Pass. A moderate face of snow, ice, and mixed steps gives a superb, accessible introduction to winter alpine climbing when conditions are right.

current.approach: Park at the upper Alpental parking lot (end of Alpental Road, shared with the Snow Lake / Source Lake trailhead). Pick up the maintained Alpental Valley trail, which runs along and above the South Fork Snoqualmie River on the old ski-area service road/cat track for about the first 0.5 mile before narrowing to a standard trail. Continue up-valley roughly 1.5-2 miles, climbing gently through forest and avalanche-path brush with Chair Peak's north side visible ahead; a boot path forks off the main Source Lake/Snow Lake trail toward Source Lake and the basin below Chair Peak's east/north aspect (~4200 ft). From the basin, ascend talus and (in season) a snow apron directly toward the base of the north face at the head of the Alpental cirque, aiming for the obvious snow/ice runnel system below the summit block. Total approach gain to the base is roughly 2,400 ft over about 2.5-3 miles one-way. Hazards: the valley floor and lower slopes cross active avalanche paths below Chair Peak, Snoqualmie Mountain, and The Tooth, so this is a serious slide-prone approach in winter/spring — most parties go early and move quickly through the runout zones; there is also a creek crossing near Source Lake that can be tricky at high flow, and the basin below the face holds a moat late-season that can complicate the final approach to the ice.
approach_variant_names: Alpental valley to the Thumb Tack, then over the northeast ridge
current.descent: From the summit, most parties reverse toward the notch/col below the summit block and descend the gully on the south side of the east face (sometimes described as the same gully used by the Northeast Buttress descent). Expect a mix of downclimbing and rappelling: parties commonly do two double-rope (60m) rappels — the first from trees/rock anchors near the head of the gully with some downclimbing to reach the next station, and a second double-rope rappel that reaches easier snow near the gully's base — though some parties describe reaching the base with a single 60m rappel plus downclimbing depending on snow coverage. Anchors are a mix of natural gear (trees, rock horns/slings) rather than bolts; bring cord/webbing to back up or replace tattered slings. From the base of the gully, downclimb snow/talus east back into the Chair Peak basin and pick up the approach trail to Source Lake and out. Watch for cornices at the gully lip early season, loose rock in the gully when snow-free, and wet-slide hazard on the descent slopes during warm spring conditions.
current.detailed_rack: A few ice screws (3-4), 2-3 pickets, slings for frequent tree-anchor belays on P2/P3, and a couple of small rock pieces or pitons for the crux step.
current.pro_needs: Screws, pickets, and a few rock pieces for the mixed step(s).

name: Northeast Buttress
beta: From the basin below Chair Peak's East Face, the route climbs a curving gully system on climber's right before trending up and left along the buttress crest to the summit. The technical crux in winter conditions is a short, steep ice bulge encountered partway up. It is commonly done in 4 pitches with a 60m rope, though many parties simul-climb sections or break it into 5-6 shorter pitches, especially in early-season snow. Short approach and moderate climbing make it very popular and prone to queues on clear winter weekends.
overview: Chair Peak's northeast buttress, at the head of the Alpental valley above Snoqualmie Pass, is a winter mixed climb: four pitches of snow, ice and easy rock, with the crux a short ice bulge on the third.

current.approach: From the upper Alpental parking lot (I-90 Exit 52, end of Alpental Road), follow the Alpental Valley/Source Lake trail: the first 0.5 mile follows the old ski-area cat track, then it becomes a standard trail climbing gently through forest for about 0.75 mile to Source Lake (roughly 1.25-1.75 miles and a few hundred feet of gain from the car). From Source Lake, leave the maintained trail and head cross-country/up boot path toward the basin below Chair Peak's east face (~4200 ft), a further 0.5-1 mile with steeper talus, heather, and (early/mid season) snow slopes. From the basin, climb a short snow gully for approximately 300 ft to gain the crest of the ridge that forms the Northeast Buttress, then follow the ridge to the start of the technical climbing. Total approach is on the order of 2-2.5 miles and 1,700-2,000 ft of gain one-way to the base of the buttress. Hazards: the basin and approach gully sit below avalanche terrain off Chair Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain — this is a classic early-season slide path, and parties often describe deep postholing, wet-slab activity, and wind-loaded slopes here; a rope/axe/crampons are typically carried from the basin onward given the exposure of the approach gully itself.
approach_variant_names: Source Lake basin to the divide (summer and fall rock)
Winter and spring, on snow
current.descent:
From the top of the buttress, scramble back across the flat summit area and drop into the first obvious gully on climber's left — not the gully further along the ridge near the true summit. Old tat on two small trees marks the entrance. The gully runs due south between high rock walls: scramble down it and take the very first left it offers, and the rappel station comes into view as soon as the walls let you out, at roughly 6,000 ft. Parties miss it by carrying on too far down, or too far right, once the gully opens up.

The station is fixed and old — three rusty pitons tied together with a mass of aging webbing and a pair of aluminium rappel rings. Two ropes give a single 60 m rappel that clears the corniced lip and lands where the gully opens out and ends; a single 60 m rope halves that and leaves 30-40 m of very steep snow to downclimb, still fully exposed to whatever comes down the gully. Move to the side of the gully mouth once you are down so the next person cannot drop anything on you. A tag line is worth carrying for exactly that reason — it buys a quick rappel to a protected stance instead of a long spell standing in the fall line.

A second gully further along is an alternative rather than a continuation: it carries both an upper and a lower anchor, so a single rope is enough to get through that one instead. Anchors on this descent are not maintained and may not be where you want them — carry cord and a knife to re-rig, and expect that getting around remaining steep snow at the base may take an extra downclimb or rappel.

Below the rappel, plunge-step or downclimb 35-40° snow to the base of the east face and traverse east to rejoin the approach. Cornice collapse at the gully lip, sloughing in warm conditions, and rock knocked down by parties above are the main descent hazards.

Rappelling the buttress itself is a documented summer alternative, taking four to five shorter rappels off a tree, a second gnarlier tree, an old pair of bolts and a rock horn.
current.detailed_rack: A single rack of nuts and cams to ~2 in, a few slings/draws, and rappel gear covers the rock route; parties attempting it as a winter line add 2-3 ice screws, a picket or two, and a second tool.
current.pro_needs: Placements are sparse on the lower scrambling terrain (roughly 2-3 solid pieces per rope-length); focus small cams and nuts on the steeper pitches, plus ice screws for the crux ice bulge in winter conditions.

name: Northwest Ridge
beta: This is a 6-pitch, 1,000 ft (303 m), Grade II, 5.7 trad route reached via the East Face approach to 'Thumbtack Rock' before angling right over the ridge. It has a low average rating (2/5 stars) reflecting run-out climbing and poor rock quality in places.
overview: A longer, sustained 5.7 ridge climb on Chair Peak, following the crest over false summits with a mix of solid and notably loose rock — the longest documented rock route on the peak by pitch count.

current.approach: Follow the East Face approach to the 'Thumbtack Rock' landmark, then head right up a grassy gully over the ridge toward the start of the Northwest Ridge.
approach_variant_names: East face approach to Thumbtack Rock, then the grassy gully over the divide
current.descent: From the true summit, traverse south across a series of false summits until reaching a tree rigged with rappel anchors at the second gully encountered heading east. Make multiple rappels down this gully to reach the East Face proper, then descend scree slopes back to Thumbtack Rock and the standard approach path.
current.detailed_rack: A single alpine rack covers the route, emphasising smaller pieces — multiple 0.4-size cams were noted as especially useful for the chockstone and crux sections. A 70 m rope is recommended for the sustained pitch lengths and to reach retreat and rappel anchors.
current.pro_needs: Protection is thin on the ridge's broken, sometimes loose rock — expect genuine runouts even on easier-looking terrain, so take every reasonable placement, especially the small cams around the chockstone and crux.

name: Voie de Chaise
beta: First climbed by Ian Nicholson and Tino Villanueva in summer/fall 2022, this 5.9- (Grade II) route climbs 8 pitches (800 ft / 242 m total, including a summit scramble) of slab and steeper rock on the East Face, protected mostly by bolts (11-12 quickdraws recommended). The crux is a 70 ft, 5.9 pitch (P5); pitches 6-7 have notably looser rock.
overview: A modern 8-pitch sport-oriented rock line up the right side of the East Face, established in 2022 — the longest fully-pitched rock route documented on Chair Peak, finishing with a short scramble to the summit.

current.approach: From the Alpental parking lot, follow the standard summer trail toward Source Lake and the East Face approach, crossing talus fields and a snow patch, then a final stretch of loose scree to the base of the route; about 2-3 hours from the parking lot.
approach_variant_names: Alpental and the Source Lake talus to the Chair snow patch, then the east face scree
current.descent: Most parties rappel the route on a single 60 m rope, using two rappel stations added in 2023. Belay the leader back down pitch 8 rather than rappelling it: rappelling it knocks loose rock onto anyone below. From the top anchor, rappel straight down to the chain anchor just right of the pitch-6 belay, then to the top of pitch 5, then down the belay stations to the ground, seven rappels in all. Several leave less than 5 ft of rope to spare, so knot the ends. If other parties are on the route, descend the East Gully instead: hike, downclimb and rappel the normal descent.
current.detailed_rack: A single 60m rope plus a second rope (or a 70m+ tag line) for the double-rope rappel descent; 11-12 quickdraws cover the mostly bolted protection, with perhaps a few small cams/nuts for belay backup.
current.pro_needs: Predominantly bolt-protected — 11-12 quickdraws is the quoted rack — which makes this notably better protected than Chair Peak's older trad lines.

name: West Ridge
beta: Established by Pro Guiding Service founder Martin Volken (first documented ascent reported July 25, 2007), the route is graded Alpine Grade 2+ / 5.7. It starts up a narrow 220 ft couloir to the low point of the ridge just east of a distinct tower (2 pitches of 5.7 to the top of the gully), then follows the ridge crest to the summit over varying rock quality and exposure.
overview: A more remote, adventurous alpine rock line up Chair Peak's west side, climbing a narrow entrance couloir to the ridge crest and then following the West Ridge to the summit — less traveled and more exposed than the Northeast Buttress.

current.approach: From the Alpental lot, follow the standard Northeast Buttress approach to the base of that buttress, then keep traversing west beneath the north face on slabby terrain that can be snowy and glide-cracked in early season to reach the base of the route, roughly 2-2.5 hours from the parking area.
approach_variant_names: Alpental and the Northeast Buttress approach, then round onto the slabs on the west side
current.descent: From the summit, descend via the standard south-side couloir, which funnels into the same narrow rappel gully used by the other Chair Peak routes; reported descent time is about 1-2 hours back to the Chair Peak basin.
current.detailed_rack: A 60m rope and a medium alpine rack.
current.pro_needs: The first 15m into the entrance couloir has no protection but stays moderate; good protection resumes on the 5.7 climbing to the ridge crest. A loose chockstone low on the route and a poorly protected 10 ft headwall are specific noted concerns.

name: Little Giant Pass – Luahna Col Route
beta: From a camp near Butterfly Butte in the Napeequa Valley, climbers travel through larch and pumice terrain, pass north of the crevassed Pilz Glacier, traverse granite slabs and tarns below Chalangin's north ridge, and gain the ridge via a scree gully around 8,000 ft before a final scramble over loose rock ("choss") to the summit. An alternate finish drops directly off Luahna Peak's west ridge to the Luahna-Chalangin col and climbs from there — reported as harder than expected, with some exposed but non-technical (Class 3) scrambling. A Forest Service description of this same trailhead/valley approach frames the target line as Chalangin's southeast ridge.
overview: A longer, higher-mileage approach via Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa River valley, skirting the north side of the Pilz Glacier to reach a gully/ridge below the Luahna-Chalangin col, then a loose Class 3 scramble to the summit; often combined with an ascent of Luahna Peak (and sometimes Clark Mountain) in the same trip.

current.approach: From the Little Giant Trailhead (2,600 ft) on Chiwawa River Road/FR 62, ford the Chiwawa River (no functional bridge; knee-to-thigh-deep, colder and higher earlier in the season) and climb the Little Giant Pass Trail through steep forest and meadows to the 6,409 ft pass on Chiwawa Ridge. Descend roughly 2,200 ft into the Napeequa River Valley and follow the Napeequa River (off-trail in its upper reaches) toward the Butterfly Butte area, camping around 6,200 ft.
approach_variant_names: Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa valley
current.descent: Downclimb the loose summit scramble to the ridge/gully, traverse back below the north ridge past the Pilz Glacier's margin, drop into and cross the Napeequa Valley, then regain Little Giant Pass (6,409 ft) and descend the trail to the Chiwawa River ford and trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: No fixed rock protection is documented as necessary; the summit scramble is unroped Class 3 on loose rock. A rope is prudent given the Pilz Glacier's crevassing.
current.pro_needs: Glacier travel kit (rope, crevasse-rescue gear) for the Pilz Glacier margin; no technical rock protection is used on the standard scramble line.
bivy: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
Napeequa Valley floor near Louis Creek

name: Southwest Face
beta: From a high camp in Chalangin Basin (~5,100 ft), climbers ascend the open south slope/southwest face of the peak, passing through a rocky cliff band around 5,500-6,500 ft (one or two 4th-class moves), then traverse snow slopes above the Pilz Glacier before a cramponed finish (accounts describe the final push variously as the south slope, southwest face, or southeast face depending on the exact line and year's snow coverage) to the summit. This is reported as the shortest-distance, least-elevation-gain of the three known approaches to Chalangin.
overview: The peak's shortest and most direct line: a long valley approach up the White River and Thunder Creek to a high camp in Chalangin Basin, followed by a snow/scramble climb up the open south slope and southwest face, through a short cliff band, to the summit.

current.approach: From the White River Trailhead (2,300 ft, end of White River Road/FR 6400), follow White River Trail #1507 to the Boulder Creek Trail junction, then continue toward Thunder Creek. Leave the trail and bushwhack up the Thunder Creek drainage (a thigh-deep creek crossing is typical in late spring), through slide alder and a 2023 burn zone (Airplane Lake Fire) with blowdowns, to a high camp/basin around 5,100 ft (Chalangin Basin) below the Luahna-Chalangin col.
current.descent: Downclimb the south slope/southwest face (same snow/scramble terrain, including the loose cliff band around 5,500-6,500 ft) back into Chalangin Basin, then retrace the Thunder Creek bushwhack and White River Trail to the trailhead; some parties vary the exit via Lower Thunder Meadows.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard line. A rope and light crevasse-rescue kit are prudent only if a variation strays onto the crevassed margin of the Pilz Glacier.
current.pro_needs: Standard glacier/steep-snow protection (ice axe, crampons); no fixed or removable rock protection is documented as necessary on the standard south-slope/southwest-face line.

name: Cheap Beer
beta: Climbs a line of seams up the middle of the steep main face: thin boulder climbing up a steep wall to a small overhang, then a few big moves on good holds before easier terrain and the anchors, which are shared with the adjacent Firearms.
overview: The hardest and best-rated route at the Minidike (also called the "Local Boys" wall), the second route encountered on the approach.

current.approach: From Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, continue ~1.5 mi to the Minidike pull-out on the left (SE) side after the river bridge; this is the second route encountered on the trail.
current.descent: Lower directly from the anchor (shared with Firearms) to the ground.
current.detailed_rack: 9 quickdraws, 30m+ rope.
current.pro_needs: Bolts to a shared chain anchor; standard sport rack.

name: Chelan Butte Trail
beta: The summit can be reached either by hiking the Chelan Butte Trail from a WDFW trailhead on the south side of the town of Chelan (via Iowa Ave, roughly 7.46 mi round trip with 2,500 ft gain) or by driving/walking Chelan Butte Road from the Millard St trailhead in the Lakeside community (4.5 mi one-way, paved for the first 1.2 mi then dirt/gravel). Both converge on the same summit-road system. A bench at the Elephant Head viewpoint offers a rest stop partway up. The route is fully exposed to sun with essentially no shade.
overview: A steep dirt-road/trail walk-up (or drive) up the grassy, exposed south flank of Chelan Butte to a summit crowned by communications towers, with 360-degree views over Lake Chelan, the Columbia River, and the surrounding Chelan/Entiat/Wenatchee Mountains. There is no technical climbing on this route.

current.approach: From the town of Chelan, take SR 150 (E Woodin Rd), then Sanders St, Farnham St, S. Saunders St, and E. Iowa Ave to the WDFW Chelan Butte trailhead parking lot, and climb the Chelan Butte Trail directly toward the summit. Alternatively, from Highway 97A at Millard Street in Lakeside (between mileposts 232-233), follow Chelan Butte Road as it climbs the west side of the butte, staying on the road or the marked hiking-trail cutoff about 1/4 mile in.
current.descent: Descend the same trail or road used on the way up, passing back through the Elephant Head viewpoint area to the trailhead. No technical downclimbing or rappelling is involved; watch footing on loose gravel and ruts on the road sections, especially after rain or snowmelt.

name: East Face (Rebel Yell area / standard)
beta: Rebel Yell is a well-established North Cascades classic featuring 7 pitches of alpine trad climbing (5.10 overall with the 5.10b crux on P5). The route climbs the clean east face via splitter cracks with varied techniques. All pitches are led on gear. Descent via 4 double-rope rappels on fixed anchors. Extra gear can be cached at base. Typically done as 2-day expedition.
overview: Chianti Spire is the second Wine Spire north of Silver Star's summit, standing between Burgundy Spire (north) and Pernod/Chablis (south). Its East Face carries the area's best-known moderate testpiece, commonly called 'East Face' or 'Rebel Yell' — a sustained, 6-to-7-pitch splitter crack climb (depending on which start you take) through every crack size from fingers to offwidth, finishing on an exposed summit block. It shares the same long, steep Burgundy Col approach and rappel descent as the rest of the Wine Spires, and is often linked with Burgundy or Pernod Spire on a multi-summit day.

current.approach: This is the same East Face/Rebel Yell line as wa_east_face_rebel_yell, so the hike-in is identical. From the SR-20 pullout near milepost ~166 (~0.7 mile west of the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff), a steep, faint climber's trail descends to Early Winters Creek; cross the creek and follow the climber's path/talus benches switchbacking up the far side, gaining about 3,500 ft over just under 5 miles to Burgundy Col — roughly 3-4 hours car-to-col with an overnight pack. Stay climber's-left toward the obvious col notch where the boot-path braids through timber and boulders lower down. A snow patch at/near the col is the last dependable water source but is unreliable by late summer, so carry water up from the creek if climbing after midsummer. From Burgundy Col, drop a short snow/rock step and traverse south below Burgundy Spire's East Face, across a small snowy rib, onto the upper Silver Star Glacier, and around to Chianti Spire's obvious east side and the base of the route (~7,900 ft) — under an hour from a col or Larch Bench camp. Carry an ice axe for this traverse through midsummer; the snow rib and glacier margin can be firm or icy in the morning.
approach_variant_names: The Wine Spires pullout to Burgundy Col, then the snow traverse south beneath Burgundy's east face onto the Silver Star Glacier
current.descent: Same descent as the standard East Face/Rebel Yell line: rappel back down the route itself on fixed anchors rather than walking off. The usual descent is four double-rope rappels using two ropes (a single 60m may work for some stations but isn't the norm), starting from the summit block, then anchors near the top of pitch 5, then continuing stations down the route generally trending climber's-right. Anchors are fixed but should be visually checked each time — this isn't a heavily-bolted sport-style descent. Rope-snag hazard exists in the chimney/offwidth pitches. After reaching the base, reverse the Silver Star Glacier traverse and snow step back to Burgundy Col, then descend the climber's trail to Early Winters Creek and the highway — parties describe this exit as notably long and tiring relative to the climb, so plan daylight accordingly.
current.detailed_rack: Single rack of cams to #4 Camalot with doubles in the offwidth-prone sizes (#0.75, #1, #2, #3 or equivalent), a set of nuts, 12-16 slings, and two 60m ropes for the rappels.
current.pro_needs: Solid alpine trad rack with doubles through offwidth sizes (#0.75-#3); comfort placing and evaluating gear in wide cracks and on fixed rappel anchors.
bivy: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side

name: Lichen Bouquet (East Face)
beta: Established in 1989, this is the second-best-known line on Chianti's east face and a quieter alternative to Rebel Yell at a full grade easier. It starts directly below the summit, following a long left-leaning ramp up into a left-facing corner and an off-width crack; three more pitches cross Rebel Yell and gain the notch between Burgundy Spire and Chianti, and a short pitch reaches the summit up the normal route. Approach and descent logistics are identical to Rebel Yell - the same Early Winters Creek trail to Burgundy Col, the same drop and traverse beneath Burgundy Spire's east face, and a rappel-based descent. It is graded II 5.9 or III 5.9. Detail is thin: pitch lengths and total footage are not known, so this is a route for a party comfortable route-finding on an alpine face rather than following a topo.
overview: A 5.9 line on the same east face as Rebel Yell, following a long left-leaning ramp into a left-facing corner and an offwidth, then crossing Rebel Yell and continuing to the notch between Burgundy Spire and Chianti, where a short pitch on the normal route reaches the summit.

current.approach: Identical to Rebel Yell. Drive SR 20 to Washington Pass, then about 4 miles east to a wide pullout on the south side of the highway near milepost 166, at roughly 4,250 ft (about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake road, about 2 miles east of the hairpin turn). No Northwest Forest Pass is required on the highway shoulder. Descend a steep, faint scree path about 300 ft to Early Winters Creek, cross on logs, then follow the climbers' trail steeply uphill to a wooded bench at 6,400-6,600 ft - the standard low camp, with a year-round spring about 200 yards north of the trail and a seasonal spring in the sandy gully above. Above the bench the trail fades; follow cairns up loose gullies, trending right and up, into the main gully below Burgundy Col at 7,800-7,950 ft. The gully holds a roughly 40-degree snow finger into midsummer. Roughly 3.5 miles and about 3,700 ft of gain to the col in 3-4 hours. From the col, descend 200-300 ft on the south side and traverse right beneath Burgundy Spire's east face on year-round snow with seasonal rock bands until Chianti's east face is in view. Rebel Yell's dihedral is the obvious feature on the right side of the face; Lichen Bouquet's ramp starts directly below the summit and leans left. Under an hour from the col.
