approach_variant_names: The Wine Spires pullout, the bench camp and the main gully to Burgundy Col, then south on year-round snow to the ramp below the summit
current.descent: Most parties on the east face descend the way Rebel Yell parties do: from the summit pedestal, scramble to the two-bolt anchor at the southeast base of the summit block and make four double-rope rappels with two 60 m ropes back to the snow at the base of the face, trending generally to the rappeller's right and pulling the ropes carefully - the flake and offwidth features snag ropes readily. The alternative, and the one this route's finish naturally suggests, is to reverse to the notch between Burgundy Spire and Chianti and descend from there. Either way, collect gear left at the base, reverse the snow traverse north beneath Burgundy Spire's east face, and regain the 200-300 ft to Burgundy Col - much easier on firm snow than late-day slush or bare sand. Then descend the loose main gully (helmets on), rejoin the trail at the bench, and take the steep path down to Early Winters Creek, finishing with the short loose scramble back up to the highway. The sandy slabs above the bench are the most-cursed section of the whole outing; trekking poles help.
current.detailed_rack: No published rack exists for this specific line, so carry the standard Chianti east-face kit: a set of nuts, doubles of cams from finger size through #3 Camalot, and a #3.5 or #4 Camalot for the offwidth the first-ascent party describes low on the route. Add 8-10 alpine draws and several double-length slings for the long left-leaning ramp, which will generate rope drag. Two 60 m ropes are essential for the descent and for the option of escaping onto Rebel Yell's rappel line.
current.pro_needs: Standard alpine trad protection on granite: ramps, a left-facing corner and an offwidth, with no fixed gear reported on the line itself. The offwidth section will want at least one large cam. Because the route crosses Rebel Yell, the fixed anchors on that line (bolts at the top of P4 and at both ends of the P5 offwidth, plus the two-bolt station at the base of the summit block) are usable for retreat. Expect more lichen and less-travelled rock than on Rebel Yell - the route's name is a fair warning - so protect for the possibility of a loose hold.

name: North Face (Original Route, 1952)
beta: First ascensionists Joe Hieb and Art Maki approached via moraine and ice to the eastern walls of the Wine Spires group, made a roughly 250-ft rappel off the west face into the notch between Chianti and Burgundy Spires, and found the north face held the only route to the top. Two leads of unstable rock presented the main difficulties, protected with seven pitons for aid/safety, and the final moves to the tiny summit required a shoulder-stand and flipping the rope over a rock flake.
overview: The original 1952 first-ascent line up Chianti Spire, gained by rappelling into the Burgundy-Chianti notch and climbing the peak's north side on then-loose rock; now rarely repeated in favor of the East Face/Rebel Yell.

current.approach: Reached from the notch between Chianti and Burgundy Spires (gained via a rappel from the west side per the original account, or by traversing in from Burgundy Col), then climbing the north face directly to the summit.
approach_variant_names: The Wine Spires pullout to Burgundy Col, then traverse in to the Burgundy-Chianti notch
current.descent: Downclimb or make a short rappel off the summit block back onto the north face, then reverse the line to the Burgundy-Chianti notch. From the notch, traverse north on snow beneath Burgundy Spire's east face and climb the 200-300 ft back up to Burgundy Col - this re-ascent is the sting in the tail and is much easier on firm morning snow than on afternoon slush or bare, sandy rock. From the col, descend the main gully carefully; below the bench the trail is fast but relentlessly steep, and the last 300 ft up from Early Winters Creek to the highway is a short, loose scramble on scree and boulders. Trip reports are unanimous that the sand-over-slab descent above the bench is the worst part of the day; trekking poles help enormously, and a helmet should stay on because parties above you dislodge rocks in the gullies.
current.detailed_rack: A standard single alpine rack to 3 inches covers the 5.6 climbing: a set of nuts, cams from about 0.4 to 3 inches, and 6-8 alpine draws plus a couple of double-length slings for the blocky north-face features. Two 60 m ropes are the norm in the Wine Spires because every descent option in the group is rappel-based and 60 m doubles let you leave the mountain from anywhere.
current.pro_needs: Historically protected with pitons; a modern ascent would rack a standard light alpine trad rack given the moderate 5.6 grade, but no contemporary route description was found to confirm current gear beta.

name: Southeast Slopes
beta: From the Mineral Creek Trailhead, follow the Mineral Creek Trail and past the Park Lakes to the Pacific Crest Trail. Head north on the PCT along the west side of Chikamin Ridge, then leave the trail around 5,500 ft to climb southeast-facing slabs, heather benches, and a broadening gully onto the crest of Chikamin Ridge. Follow the ridge/gully system to the summit horn, finishing with a short, well-protected Class 3 chimney (about 10 ft) and roughly 75 more feet of easy scrambling to the top. An alternate approach from Glacier Lake/Chikamin Lake (via Mineral Creek and a Spectacle Point saddle) reaches the same upper mountain from the east.
overview: Chikamin Peak (6,994 ft) is a high, prominent summit on the Pacific Crest Trail divide between Snoqualmie Pass and the Lemah Mountain/Chimney Rock country, in the heart of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. It's the highest point on Chikamin Ridge, six miles northeast of Snoqualmie Pass, with sweeping views over Spectacle, Chikamin, and Glacier lakes. First climbed May 30, 1915 by C.G. Morrison and I.J. Kohler. The standard route leaves the PCT near Chikamin Pass and climbs a broad gully on the southeast slope of Chikamin Ridge, staying clear of the cliffy "Four Brothers" towers, before a short Class 3 finish to the summit horn. The long trail approach, not the climbing itself, is the main effort.

current.approach: Two established approaches reach the southeast-side gullies, and both are worth knowing since parties come at this route from either direction. (1) PCT from Snoqualmie Pass: From the PCT North Trailhead (Trail #2000) off Exit 52, the trail switchbacks up through timber and avalanche paths, crosses beneath Kendall Peak, and hits the exposed rock-cut traverse of Kendall Katwalk around mile 5 (~5,400 ft) — a good checkpoint, though don't count on water here late season. Continue north past Ridge Lake (~mile 6.5, reliable camping and water) and the Alaska Lake/Joe Lake junctions, then along the rolling, rocky PCT beneath Alaska and Huckleberry Mountains to the Huckleberry–Chikamin saddle around mile 10.25. The trail then contours below the Four Brothers and Chikamin's south face; note the Park Lakes Trail junction here, which ties in the Mineral Creek approach below. At roughly mile 13.5 — about a half-mile short of Chikamin Pass, near an established pack camp where the trail dips to about 5,500 ft — leave the PCT and climb steep grassy/heather slopes into the gully systems on the south/southeast face. Do not continue on to Chikamin Pass itself before cutting uphill: doing so puts you in the middle of the Four Brothers, a band of cliffy towers that force technical terrain. One-way distance from the trailhead to the base of the gullies is about 13.5 miles with roughly 4,600 ft of gain, so most parties camp along the PCT (Ridge Lake or the pack camp near the turnoff) and treat this as a 2–3 day trip rather than a car-to-car push. (2) Mineral Creek/Park Lakes approach: From the Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331) at the end of FR-46/Cooper Pass Road (~2,400 ft), the trail is brushy lower down but well-trodden; it climbs steadily beside Mineral Creek to Park Lakes (~4.3–5.4 mi, ~2,570 ft gain) and ties into the PCT. From the PCT/Park Lakes junction, head north toward the Spectacle Point saddle overlooking Spectacle Lake, then drop about a mile to Glacier Lake, a common camp, before climbing the southeast-slope gullies above the lake — parties describe brooks, waterfalls, tarns, heather benches, sandstone slabs and blocky breccia low down, with some exposure near the final ridge crest. This is the shortest line in (day-trip feasible for strong parties, roughly 14–16.5 mi round trip) but involves rougher tread and creek crossings lower on the trail. Either way, once above treeline the gully system itself is loose scree and dirt-and-heather slots in its upper sections — expect Class 2 hiking low, stepping up to sustained Class 3 (with a short, well-protected Class 4 chimney/slot right below the summit block on some lines) as you gain Chikamin Ridge and approach the summit horn.
approach_variant_names: PCT from Snoqualmie Pass, leaving the trail half a mile short of Chikamin Pass
Mineral Creek and Park Lakes, then the gullies above Glacier Lake
current.descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb route — no rappelling on the standard line. From the summit, reverse the ascent gully: downclimb the short crux chimney/slot below the summit block (Class 3, with one low-Class-4 move reported on some lines), then work back down the heather benches and slabs to the broad gully on the south side of Chikamin Ridge. Descend the gully itself carefully — it is loose scree and dirt underfoot, with real rockfall potential onto anyone below, so keep the group tight and go one at a time through the narrower sections — back down to the grassy slopes above the PCT. Rejoin the trail either near the pack camp at the turnoff (if you came up via Snoqualmie Pass/PCT) or continue down past Glacier Lake toward the Park Lakes/Mineral Creek trail (if using that approach), matching whichever line you climbed. Some parties have improvised alternate descents off the east ridge or down toward Chikamin Lake to the northeast; at least one party describes that variation as loose, unprotected Class 4 downclimbing requiring a hand-line/'panic rope' for security through a 6,600 ft notch — that is an exploratory off-route line, not the standard descent, and shouldn't be treated as such. No fixed anchors, bolts, or rappel stations are reported anywhere on this route. A short hand-line for the summit-block chimney is a reasonable optional safety margin for less confident scramblers, but it is not a technical rappel, and 0 rappels are needed on the standard route.
current.detailed_rack: No roped protection is used on the standard scramble line; some parties carry a short hand-line ("panic rope") to belay themselves or teammates through the crux summit chimney or on any loose downclimbing.
current.pro_needs: None required for the standard Class 2-3 line — it is unroped scrambling. A short hand-line for the summit chimney/any loose sections is a common precaution rather than a necessity.
bivy: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
Ridge Lake / Gravel Lake saddle camps
current.rope_note: Off-trail Class 2-3 scramble over talus, slabs, and heather; exposure only on the final ridge crest. No rope typically used; helmet recommended for rockfall/exposure.

name: Standard Route
beta: Chimney Peak has no maintained trail to its summit. Parties approach via the long East Fork Quinault River backpack to Enchanted Valley Chalet, then travel off-trail north/northeast into the basin below the peak's southwest side, gain the southwest ridge, and follow class 3 terrain to the summit. The peak's south side is defined by very steep, waterfall-streaked cliffs (~4,800 ft of relief above the valley in under a mile), so route-finding onto moderate ground on the SW ridge/gully system is the key to keeping the climb at class 3. A separate, harder objective — "The Chimney," a ~100-ft rock tower on the peak's west aspect — was first climbed in 1970 at class 5.3 and is not part of this standard scramble line.
overview: Chimney Peak (6,917 ft, correcting the older 6,913 ft figure) is a rugged, remote summit in the central Olympics on the west side of the Mount Anderson massif (parent peak West Peak, 7,365 ft, 3.4 mi NE). It sits immediately north above Enchanted Valley, the "Valley of Ten Thousand Waterfalls," with over 4,800 ft of relief rising from the valley floor in less than a mile. The peak's name comes from "The Chimney," a 100-ft rock tower on its west aspect first climbed (5.3) by Mike Banner and Vern Johnson in 1970; the mountain was originally called "Old Snowback" and its summit was first reached in 1941 by Tolvo J. Nelson. The standard ascent follows the southwest ridge on Class 3-4 terrain with loose rock and real exposure near the top.

current.approach: From the Graves Creek Trailhead in the SW corner of Olympic National Park, follow the East Fork Quinault River Trail (Enchanted Valley Trail) east. The first roughly 2 miles follow an old roadbed through big firs and cedar before a short, steep drop to river level; at 2.5 miles the trail crosses Pony Bridge, a narrow, photogenic span over a fern-lined gorge — a reliable early water source before the long valley slog. From there the trail undulates through old-growth rainforest (spruce, alder, maple) to O'Neil Creek Camp at about mile 6.7, then crosses No Name Creek and Pyrites Creek around miles 8–9.5 (Pyrites has camps on both banks, ~12 sites total, and is a good staging point for a two-day approach). Beyond Pyrites the trail climbs gently for several more miles, including a high bridge roughly 20 ft above the river that can feel exposed if snow-covered early season. Around mile 13 the trail opens into Enchanted Valley (~2,000 ft) at the historic chalet, directly beneath Chimney Peak's southeast face, which rears 4,800 ft above the valley floor in under a mile — far too steep and cliff-bound for the standard route. From the valley (climbers appear to peel off the maintained trail somewhat short of the chalet, roughly mid-valley), leave the trail and work cross-country around the mountain's south/southwest flank — brushy, unmarked, boulder-and-timber route-finding with no cairns — up a drainage that gains the SW ridge crest, where the Class 3 scrambling begins. Given the 13-mile one-way trail approach, most parties camp in the valley (Pyrites Creek or Enchanted Valley) and climb the peak as a long day from camp rather than car-to-car.
current.descent: Descend by reversing the SW ridge scramble line back toward the valley — the same Class 3 terrain used on ascent — since the peak's cliff-girt southeast and north aspects offer no easier walk-off. Downclimbing is straightforward for a competent scrambling party, but loose rock and fast-forming cloud (the Olympics sock in quickly) make route-finding the main hazard; stay well back from the southeast face's edge, which drops 4,800 ft to Enchanted Valley in under a mile. Parties less comfortable reversing the short exposed step(s) low on the ridge sometimes opt for one short, single-rope rappel off a natural anchor (sling around a horn or block — no fixed bolts or chains are documented for this route) rather than downclimb it; a single 30–60m rope is more than sufficient. Treat this as an optional, situational rappel rather than a mandatory one — many parties downclimb the whole ridge. Once back to valley-floor terrain, work cross-country back to the Enchanted Valley Trail and reverse the ~13-mile trail hike to Graves Creek Trailhead, re-crossing Pyrites Creek, No Name Creek, and Pony Bridge.
current.detailed_rack: Light rack (small-to-mid cams/nuts) and a rope to protect or belay the exposed Class 3-4 crest of the southwest ridge near the summit. Parties who also want the separate "Chimney" tower (5.3) on the west face should bring a standard trad rack for that pitch — it is not needed for the walk-up summit route.
current.pro_needs: Minimal alpine pro; belay exposed steps as needed
bivy: Pyrites Creek — where the Chimney Peak approach leaves the trail

name: East Face Direct
beta: Solid 5.6 climbing that rejoins the East Face route about halfway up. Instead of the standard route's loose rock, this variation deals with a moat, which parties cross by building a snow anchor with a picket and jumping the gap. Nine pitches in all, mostly fourth class with short easy fifth-class steps.
overview: A harder, more direct 1954 variation of the East Face that climbs solid 5.6 rock through the lower face — avoiding the loose ('choss') sections of the standard route at the cost of a moat crossing — before rejoining the East Face about halfway up.

current.approach: Same as the standard East Face: Pete Lake Trailhead (2,800 ft) via Pete Lake Trail/PCT and the Chimney Creek climber's path to high camp at Sunrise Knob (~4,600-4,800 ft).
approach_variant_names: Pete Lake and the Chimney Creek climbers' path, then straight up the glacier under the summit
current.descent: Once the route rejoins the standard East Face partway up, descend as for that route: downclimb/rappel with a single rope, carrying spare webbing for old anchors.
current.detailed_rack: Single rack (nuts/cams), tat and webbing for rappelling.
current.pro_needs: Single rack, nuts, tat and webbing for the rappels, and a knife to cut away old tat and pack it out.
bivy: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps

name: South Peak via East Gully
beta: From the upper Chimney Glacier, cross the moat at the foot of the rock and climb the face to the left of the main gully that drops from the notch between the central and south summits. About three pitches of wet, slippery fourth-class ground lead to a system of ledges, some of them very wide, that runs up to just below the notch, roughly 600 vertical ft above the glacier. From the notch, climb about 400 ft more to the South Peak. Stoppers and slings are enough protection.
overview: Chimney Rock is a steep peak on the Cascade Crest in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness with three summits: the central spire (7,727 ft) is the highest, the north peak is 7,634 ft, and the minor south peak is 7,440 ft. This line climbs the south peak. From the Chimney Glacier it takes wet fourth-class ground and ledges up the east side to the notch between the central and south summits, then continues about 400 ft to the top.

current.approach: This route shares the same trailhead-to-basin approach as the East Face: from the Pete Lake Trailhead off FR 4616, hike the Pete Lake Trail #1323 (~4 easy miles to Pete Lake, then ~2 more miles) to the Pacific Crest Trail junction, head north on the PCT about a mile to the Chimney Creek avalanche-path crossing, then leave the PCT and follow the climber's path (flagged/cairned, fords Chimney Creek and crosses several brushy ravines) up through Sunrise Knob (~4,650 ft, ~4-5 hrs from the trailhead) to the moraine and the bivy basin at the toe of the Chimney Glacier (~5,400 ft) — see the East Face route's approach text for full turn-by-turn detail on this shared stretch, and treat it as a 2-3 day car-to-car trip. Above camp, a wet, grubby gully through the rock band leads onto the upper Chimney Glacier; rope up, cross toward the gully below the notch between the central and south summits, and be ready to improvise around the moat at the foot of the rock, which gets worse later in the season. Water and camping options match the East Face approach: Pete Lake, the low Chimney Creek crossings, or melted glacier snow above the moraine.
approach_variant_names: Chimney Glacier to the East Gully
current.descent: Descend the line of ascent. From the South Peak, return about 400 ft to the notch between the central and south summits, then follow the ledge system back down; the ledges are easy to pick out from above. Rappel the steeper, wet fourth-class steps on a single 60 m rope rather than downclimbing them. No fixed anchors are known on this line, so carry slings, cord and a few rap rings to build and leave your own. Cross the moat back onto the glacier, reverse the glacier and the gully through the rock band, and return to camp.
current.detailed_rack: A small set of stoppers and a handful of slings in several lengths protects the wet fourth-class pitches and builds rappel anchors; add cord and rap rings to leave behind.
rack: Cord and rap rings for rappel anchors
current.pro_needs: Stoppers and slings are enough for the fourth-class pitches; a single 60 m rope covers the climbing and the rappels on the way down.
bivy: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
current.rope_note: A single 60 m rope covers the fourth-class pitches to the notch and the single-rope rappels over the steeper steps on the way down.

name: Chitlins Con Carne
beta: No detailed move-by-move description of this route has been written down; it is on record as sharing its start with Caravan, which breaks right after the 3rd bolt — Chitlins is presumed to continue more directly.
overview: A bolted face route at Summertime Crag that shares its start with the neighboring Caravan before finishing on its own line.

current.approach: Summertime Crag uses a different trailhead than the other four areas' shared Blue Lake approach. From Winthrop, drive west on SR-20 through Mazama toward Washington Pass (or, coming from Seattle, continue past Washington Pass toward Mazama on SR-20); park at a small pullout on the east side of the highway, just before the larger 'Spires Gully' parking area used to access the Early Winters Spires from the east. From the pullout, descend off the road down through trees, cross Early Winters Creek, follow it briefly downstream, then climb up-slope and contour left to reach the crag — about a 20-25 minute walk with minimal elevation change. The crag stays shaded until mid-afternoon in summer, making it a popular warm-weather alternative when Mazama-area cragging runs hot.
current.descent: Lower or make a single-rope rappel from the top anchor back to the base; reverse the approach to return to the car.
current.detailed_rack: Protection details are not documented on the route's own page; given the route type (sport) and its shared start with the fully-bolted Caravan, a standard quickdraw rack is likely sufficient, but confirm before climbing.
current.pro_needs: Not documented in detail; assume bolted per route type until confirmed on-site.

name: Southwest Route / Standard
beta: Ascend the southwest snowfield and scree slopes to reach the summit at 8,459 feet. The route follows the path of least resistance from Fortress-Chiwawa Col, traversing east-northeast aiming for the col, then ascending the final south ridge. Navigate snow or scree to within 100 feet of the summit, then traverse the west side to avoid steep rock sections on the final approach.
overview: Chiwawa Mountain (8,459') is a remote summit in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. Its parent peak, Fortress Mountain (8,760'), lies about 1.1 miles west across the Fortress-Chiwawa col, and the two are commonly combined from a shared high camp. A small remnant of the Lyman Glacier clings to Chiwawa's northeast slope above Lyman Lake, but that is a separate, more involved approach on the far side of the mountain; the standard southwest route described here is a non-glaciated, largely cross-country scramble (Class 2-3) up scree, heather, and early-season snow to the west ridge, finishing on cairned Class 2 terrain to the summit. First climbed in 1921 by a Mountaineers party led by Lorenz A. Nelson.

current.approach: Park at Trinity Trailhead (~2,800 ft), at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 by the old Trinity mine site. From the trailhead, hike the Buck Creek Trail #1513 up the valley; at roughly 1.4–1.5 miles, bear right (northeast) at the junction onto the Chiwawa River Trail #1550, an old mining-road grade that continues up-valley along the river (reliable water the whole way here). Follow the Chiwawa River Trail about 3.7 more miles to the signed Red Mountain Trail junction at Chiwawa Mountain's southeastern foot — roughly 5 miles and the last easy, obvious water before the basin. Most parties bear left here into Chiwawa Basin rather than taking the right-hand switchbacks up Red Mountain. The tread beyond the junction is rougher and sometimes braided; it climbs about a mile-plus through forest and then subalpine meadow toward the ~5,500 ft basin below the Fortress-Chiwawa col. Expect a shallow ford of the Chiwawa River/headwater creek in this stretch, and favor the more open, less-timbered ground along the east side of the basin to avoid brush-whacking. Above the basin, gain the ~6,300 ft bench via talus/scree gullies or vegetated slopes just left of them — early-season parties will find snow gullies here (ice axe/crampons recommended) that are faster than the loose summer scree. From the bench, the standard finish is a class 2 scramble up slabs and gullies on the southwest face; the short section gaining the summit ridge is the route's crux — loose, exposed class 2–3 rock — after which an easy ~100 ft rightward (west) traverse leads to the summit. One-way distance from Trinity is roughly 7–8 miles with about 5,700 ft of gain; most parties camp in Chiwawa Basin or on the 6,300 ft bench and treat it as an overnight, though fit parties do it car-to-car in a long day. A less-traveled alternate approach starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead, bushwhacking to about 5,500 ft and following a gully right of Point 5971 up to the col west of the summit, then easy Class 2 along the west ridge.
approach_variant_names: Trinity and the Chiwawa River Trail to Chiwawa Basin and the 6,300 ft benches
Phelps Creek variant to the col west of the summit
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down the southwest scree/gully slopes to the 6,300 ft bench, staying off the looser climber's-left skyline gully in favor of the main descent gullies/vegetated slopes used on the way up. Continue down into Chiwawa Basin, re-ford the creek, and retrace the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 and Buck Creek Trail #1513 back to the Trinity Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling anywhere on it — none is typically required. Watch for loose rock and scree underfoot on the upper southwest slopes (a common complaint on nearby Fortress Mountain's gullies applies here too), and in early season the same gullies used for the ascent can be glissaded or skied for a much faster descent when snow-covered.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed on the standard Class 2-3 line. A rope/small rack only comes into play if combining with Fortress Mountain's Class 3-4 east ridge, or if you stray off the cairned line into the low-5th-class gully some parties have mistakenly followed.
current.pro_needs: Non-technical Class 2-3 scramble on the standard line; an ice axe covers firm snow on the approach and col through early-mid summer. No rope, rack, or crevasse-rescue gear is needed on this side of the mountain unless you detour onto the glaciated NE (Lyman Glacier) side or add Fortress Mountain's Class 3-4 east ridge.
bivy: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds

name: Chockstone Route
beta: A low-fifth-class slab/layback step leads into gully hiking (often holding snow early season) toward the giant chockstone. A 5.7 pitch bypasses the chockstone on the left via blocky terrain and an exposed lieback, historically protected by old pitons, finishing on a delicate slab with sparse bolt protection. Moderate climbing on golden rock with modern bolts, a rightward traverse, and a final loose gully/chimney lead to the summit plateau.
overview: Chockstone Route (II+ 5.7) climbs the gully and south face between North and South Early Winters Spire — the original 1950 first-ascent line up the peak. A low-angle slab/layback first pitch (often scrambled or simul-climbed) leads up the gully toward a massive chockstone, bypassed on the left via the 5.7 crux pitch, before chimney systems lead to the summit plateau.

current.approach: From the Blue Lake Trailhead (5,400 ft) on SR-20, follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the climbers' path, leave the trail into the basin below the Liberty Bell Group, and locate the obvious chasm/gully between North and South Early Winters Spire on the west side of the formations. Allow 1-2 hours car-to-base; expect to switch between rock shoes and boots/crampons if snow lingers in the gully.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail to the chasm between the two spires
current.descent: The standard descent uses four bolted rappel stations with a 60m rope, plus one rappel off a tree down the 5.0 slab near the start, located about 30m down and skier's-right of the summit exit. An older/original variant instead makes five rappels straight down the ascent gully, including one free-hanging rappel off the chockstone, through loose and windy terrain; this is considered slower and less pleasant than the bolted West Face option.
current.detailed_rack: A single cam rack from 0.5-2in plus a nut set covers the route; bring extra quickdraws for the fixed pins and bolts on the crux and upper pitches.
current.pro_needs: Protection is adequate on the crux 5.7 pitch, but the original fixed pitons here date to the 1940s-50s and should be backed up rather than trusted outright; modern bolts on the upper pitches are more reliable.
current.rope_note: 60m rope for the rappel descent: 4 bolted rap stations plus one tree rappel down the 5.0 slab at the very start of the route. Bring an ice axe (and crampons if snow lingers) for the entry gully in early season.

name: Walrus Glacier
beta: Most parties camp at Boulder Basin and climb Clark as a two-day (sometimes three-day) trip. From camp, drop over Boulder Pass to a bench on Clark's eastern arm, gain the Walrus Glacier, and ascend a moderately steep chute on the glacier's left (south) margin, stepping over narrow crevasses and crossing at least one snow-bridge, to a short summit scramble. A glacier-free alternative (the 'Southeast Route') avoids the glacier via a gully out of the south basin but is not the line documented here.
overview: Clark Mountain (8,602 ft) is the highest summit of the Dakobed Range, rising about 8 miles southeast of Glacier Peak at the head of the Boulder Creek/White River, Napeequa, and Chiwawa drainages within the Glacier Peak Wilderness. The mountain's south and west sides are open, rugged scree and heather slopes, while its glaciated north and east flanks carry the small Clark (Walrus) Glacier and the Richardson Glacier. Luahna Peak, about a mile northwest along the connecting ridge, is a common add-on for strong parties. Two standard lines are climbed: a non-glacier scree/Class 3 scramble up the south side, and the more scenic Walrus Glacier route approached from Boulder Pass, often called one of the most esthetic non-technical glacier climbs in the eastern Cascades.

current.approach: Start at the White River Trailhead (~2,300 ft, end of White River Road/FR-6400). Follow White River Trail #1507 south along the flat valley floor for about 4 miles - easy grade but notoriously buggy/mosquito-heavy in early-to-mid summer - to its junction with Boulder Creek Trail #1562. Turn onto Boulder Creek Trail and climb roughly 4.5 miles through forest into Boulder Creek Basin, fording Boulder Creek (unbridged) around 4,000 ft; in early season this crossing is cold and knee-to-thigh deep and sometimes braids into two or three separate channels. Established camps sit in the open basin between about 4,900 and 5,300 ft (roughly 8.5 miles and ~3,000 ft of gain from the car), and given the scale of this outing (~22-23 miles round trip, 6,200-6,500+ ft one-way gain to the summit) most parties treat this as a base camp rather than a car-to-car day. From camp, leave the maintained trail and climb open heather/talus north toward Boulder Pass (~6,300 ft) - a direct fall-line push from about 5,800 ft takes roughly 1.5 hours. Two lines diverge from the pass area: for the glacier line, go down steep snow on the far side of the pass and climb to a bench near 6,700 ft on Clark's eastern arm, and rope up there for crevassed glacier travel (crampons and axe required); then traverse east across the basin under Peak 7242, crossing its NE ridge near 6,700 ft, then turn west (~30 min) to reach the toe of the Walrus Glacier (marked 'Clark Glacier' on some maps). For the non-glacier south-basin alternative, stay climber's-left, gain the south ridge of Pt. 8373 on open heather, and locate the single easy gully near 7,200-7,300 ft breaching the summit rock band; contour broken rock and lingering snow to the final south/west ridge and a short class 3 scramble to the summit. Water is reliable along the White River and in Boulder Creek Basin but essentially absent above camp - fill up before the push. Key hazards: the unbridged Boulder Creek ford, heavy mosquitoes on the valley approach, wet-slide/avalanche-prone slopes on the basin traverse into early summer, and genuine route-finding difficulty picking the correct gully/ridge above the basin - parties have gotten cliffed out searching for it.
approach_variant_names: Boulder Creek and the sheepherder's trail to the south basin — the non-glacier line
Boulder Pass and the Walrus Glacier — the glacier line
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line back to Boulder Creek Basin camp, then out via Boulder Creek Trail #1562 and White River Trail #1507 to the trailhead. If you climbed via the Walrus Glacier, descend the same glacier line back down to the 6,700 ft bench and over Boulder Pass, staying roped through the crevassed sections and unroping once back on stable moraine/talus below the ice. If you climbed/are descending the non-glacier south-basin alternative, downclimb the same class 3-4 gully and ridge terrain you ascended back to the heather slopes above camp. Watch for lingering wet-snow avalanche debris on the basin traverse below Boulder Pass in early/mid-summer, and re-ford Boulder Creek on the way out. This is fundamentally a long walk-off/scramble descent, not a rappel-dependent one.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed; this is a glacier scramble rather than a roped rock climb. A rope for the team, a few ice screws, and slings/carabiners for the Walrus Glacier crossing, where narrow crevasses and at least one snow-bridge are typically encountered.
current.pro_needs: Glacier-travel and crevasse-rescue gear rather than rock protection: a rope, crevasse-rescue hardware, ice axe, and crampons for the glacier chute. No fixed or removable rock protection is typically placed on the Class 3 scrambling sections above the glacier.
bivy: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
current.rope_note: Route crosses the Walrus (Clark) Glacier before a Class 3 rock finish to the summit. Rope up for glacier travel; standard crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks) recommended. Rock finish from the ~8000' col is typically done unroped.

name: Classic Route
beta: A single, easy blocky low-5th-class pitch up the summit block/'horn,' reached via the standard Snow Lake / Unicorn Creek approach. Considered fun in mixed/early-season conditions and a reasonable solo for confident scramblers, though most parties rope up.
overview: The most-travelled line up Unicorn's summit block: one easy, blocky low-5th-class pitch up the south-southeast face of the horn.

current.approach: Start at the Snow Lake Trailhead on Stevens Canyon Road (~1.5 miles east of Reflection Lakes, elev. ~4,500 ft). Follow the maintained Snow Lake Trail about 1.25 miles, with roughly 350 ft of up-and-down, to Snow Lake at ~4,600 ft — the last reliable water source. Skirt the west/north shore of the lake; the maintained tread continues a short way over a tree-covered rise before petering out into talus. From there work up and right toward an obvious talus/dirt gully on the peak's NW side — a climbers' path picks up again on a heather bench near the top of the gully. Follow this into the basin below Unicorn Peak, ascending moraine along the left (south) side of the small permanent snow patch/glacier remnant in the basin (crampons/an axe are handy in early season on the couloir above, though not strictly required most of the year). A climbers' path traverses below the cliffs here, offering easier travel than the loose scree and talus on either side, and leads up to the saddle (Unicorn Col) just west of the summit. From the saddle, a use trail traverses east/around the south side of the main summit block, across a final loose scree slope, to the base of the summit horn. Total approach is roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way with about 2,400 ft of gain; expect route-finding through talus and some loose rock once off the maintained trail, and possible steep snow in the gully/basin into mid-summer.
approach_variant_names: Snow Lake and Unicorn Col to the middle line on the summit horn
current.descent: Downclimb or rappel back down the same south-face line you climbed. The rappel anchor is a large rock horn on the south side of the summit block (a bleached/dead tree or snag was used historically — that anchor is no longer sound and should not be trusted; use the rock horn, which parties describe as backed with slings/webbing and sometimes rappel rings). This is a single-rope rappel of roughly 40-50 ft down the pinnacle's south face; a 30m rope is generally described as enough to both lead the route and make the rappel, though at least one party found a 30m rope fell just short and recommended a 37-40m rope to be safe, and notes there are effectively two rappel options from the top — one drops directly to the notch/ground below the horn, the other lands you on the glacier/snow patch side, so confirm which station you're using and its exact length before committing. After the rappel (or downclimb, which is a viable option for confident 4th/low-5th-class scramblers but notably exposed), reverse the approach: back across the scree slope and around to the saddle, down through the basin and gully to Snow Lake, then out the Snow Lake Trail to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: One fixed piton mid-pitch plus a single set of nuts is sufficient; a few small cams are optional.
current.pro_needs: Minimal rack — small-to-mid cams/nuts and slings for a short crack plus natural horn/boulder anchors; no bolts on route.
bivy: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
current.rope_note: One of ~4 established lines on Unicorn Peak's ~50ft south summit-block face, graded 5.4. Short face means a single 30m rope usually suffices, though it can come up just short on the rappel.

name: Classic Route
beta: From Reflection Lake, follow the Pinnacle Peak trail up onto the Tatoosh Range crest, then pick up a climbers' path heading west toward Lane Peak; alternatively, approach from Narada Falls, crossing Tatoosh Creek and climbing the gully between Lane and Denman Peaks to the ~5,440 ft Lane-Denman saddle. Technical climbing begins on the east face (~46.7578, -121.7523), alternating exposed scrambling and short protected steps through loose rock, using a sturdy tree roughly 200 ft up as the main anchor, to a small summit perch with views of Rainier, Adams, and St. Helens.
overview: Also known as the South Face route, this is Lane Peak's non-technical standard line and the descent for the north-face couloirs. From the Tatoosh Creek drainage it climbs the broad talus/gully separating Lane and Denman Peaks, finishing with a narrow, sustained 3rd-class summit gully that has a few 4th-class moves; a fixed sling is often in place there for a handline or short rappel. It's commonly combined with an easy traverse east to Denman and Plummer Peaks along the Tatoosh crest.

current.approach: Start from the Reflection Lake pullout on Stevens Canyon Road (open roughly Memorial Day through mid-October) or, when the road is gated by snow, from the Narada Falls pullout — from Narada Falls a short, steep ~200 ft climb through open timber gets you up to Stevens Canyon Road. From either start, walk the road roughly half a mile to the point where it bends sharply and begins heading east; leave the pavement here and drop south through sparse, open forest toward Tatoosh Creek, losing a couple hundred feet to reach it around 4,500 ft. Cross the creek (a rock-hop most of the season, more involved during peak snowmelt) and angle up onto a broad talus slope — about 250 vertical feet — that runs down to the creek (snow-covered in spring, boulder-hopping by mid/late summer). At the top of the talus, continue up through trees staying right of a short cliff band (the timber here is brushy and it's easy to drift toward the cliff if you're not paying attention). Roughly 700 ft above the creek crossing (~5,200 ft) you break out of the trees onto open slopes and continue up to the broad 5,440 ft saddle between Lane Peak and Denman Peak. From the saddle, turn right (west) and climb moderate open ground aiming for the obvious gully weakness in the southeast face — this is the 'prominent gully' the route is named for. Follow it up, trending left near the top for the final short scramble (mostly Class 3 with plentiful holds, plus a few exposed 4th-class moves) to the 6,012 ft summit. Round trip from the road is a bit over 3 miles with roughly 1,400-1,500 ft of gain; there is no reliable water past Tatoosh Creek. Hazards: spring snow/avalanche debris and wet rock in the creek drainage and talus, brushy route-finding through the timber band, and loose rock / rockfall exposure in the summit gully, especially with parties above.
approach_variant_names: Tatoosh Creek, the timber band and the Lane-Denman saddle
current.descent: This is mostly a downclimb; the sturdy tree in the gully allows an optional rappel over the loosest section. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the summit scramble and the southeast-face gully back to the 5,440 ft Lane–Denman saddle, then drop east back through the timber (staying right of the cliff band on the way down, mirroring the ascent line) to the top of the talus slope. Descend the talus to Tatoosh Creek, re-cross, and climb back up to Stevens Canyon Road, then walk back to the Narada Falls or Reflection Lake pullout. Watch for loose rock and inconsistent glissade conditions in the gully (plunge-stepping is fine on consolidated snow but the gully holds loose rock once it melts out), and take care not to cliff yourself out in the timber band by drifting off the ascent line.
current.detailed_rack: Not worth carrying a trad rack aside from a few slings for the tree anchor around 200 ft up; the terrain is mostly unprotected scrambling on loose rock.
current.pro_needs: Minimal — the fixed/natural tree anchor is the only reliable protection; the route is essentially soloed.
bivy: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
current.rope_note: No route-specific beta found for a route named 'Classic Route' on Lane Peak; likely the south-side 3rd-4th class walk-up scramble. Typically climbed unroped by competent parties; a short rope/handline is a reasonable option for the class 4 sections.

name: Clast from the Past
beta: P1 (5.5) climbs about 100 ft up slabby rock on 7 bolts to a chain anchor; P2 (5.10c/d) continues about 80 ft on 9 bolts through the route's crux, pulling a roof near the top. Rated 5.10b overall. It shares the same lichen-covered basalt band as Sidewinder but follows it up and to the left rather than traversing right.
overview: A two-pitch bolted line up the left (west) side of Pinto Rock's north-facing basalt band, with an easy warm-up pitch leading to a harder roof-pull finish.

current.approach: From Randle, WA on US Hwy 12: head south on SR 131, then follow NF-25 for 19.2 miles; just past milepost 21, turn left at the Mosquito Meadows sign onto NF-28 for 2.7 miles; turn left onto NF-77 (rough gravel, drive slowly) for about 2 miles until Pinto Rock comes into view at a large pullout. An evident use trail leads north from the pullout to the base of the formation (~0.3 mi/0.47 km). For North Side, hike around the formation's east side to the base, or summit and rappel the fixed rings to reach the route.
current.descent: From the P2 anchor, rappel ~80 ft to the P1 chain anchor, then rappel ~100 ft to the ground — both raps are within single-rope (60m) range.
current.detailed_rack: Sport rack: 16-18 quickdraws to cover both pitches (7 bolts + anchor on P1, 9 bolts + anchor on P2) plus a 60m rope for the rappels.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted two-pitch sport route; no trad gear required, just enough draws for both pitches and anchors.
current.rope_note: Two-pitch basalt route on the North Side of Pinto Rock; a single 60m rope is enough for both rappels.
